title: When Do Interbank Market Asymmetries Disappear? Evidence from CBDC Models
affiliations: and Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: When Do Interbank Market Asymmetries Disappear? Evidence from CBDC Models
detail.abstract: We characterize the conditions under which asymmetries in interbank markets collapse, and show that this occurs only when both matching frictions and corridor-based policy wedges are absent. Across three distinct modeling environments-efficient matching, a zero standing-facility corridor, and reduced two-type banking structures-the steady state converges to the same set of interest-rate equalities linking interbank, lending, and deposit rates to the return on reserves. This convergence arises despite substantial differences in the underlying frictions. The analysis clarifies when three-type bank heterogeneity can emerge and shows that non-participation requires either matching inefficiency or a positive policy corridor. These findings refine the theoretical foundations of interbank market modeling in CBDC frameworks and help explain why seemingly different models often deliver identical steady-state outcomes.

title: The Output Gap: Method Choice, Data Revisions, and Policy Implications
affiliations: University of Wisconsin - Milwaukee

detail.title: The Output Gap: Method Choice, Data Revisions, and Policy Implications
detail.abstract: This paper compares eight widely used methods for estimating the output gap, ranging from simple deterministic trends to state space models, using both revised and real time U.S. quarterly data from 1980 onward. The resulting measures differ heavily across approaches. Average gap estimates vary by nearly four percentage points, volatility differs by an order of magnitude, and correlations across methods span from strongly positive to negative. Stability across data vintages also varies substantially. Hamilton type filters show relatively strong agreement between real time and final estimates, while simpler trend based methods are considerably less stable. These differences matter for empirical inference. The choice of output gap measure has important implications for Phillips curve estimates and for forecasting performance. Beveridge Nelson decompositions display strong predictive power for inflation when estimated using revised data but perform less well in real time, whereas refined Beveridge Nelson and modified Hamilton filters deliver more consistent results across vintages. Time varying analysis shows that the relationship between economic slack and inflation strengthens during periods of macroeconomic stress, including the early 1990s recession, the global financial crisis, and the post-pandemic period, rather than declining monotonically. For output growth forecasting, HP filter gaps reduce forecast errors using revised data, while unobserved components models perform best in real time. Although Beveridge Nelson based measures are informative for inflation, they tend to worsen growth forecasts. Combining forecasts across gap measures, particularly using Bates Granger weights, yields more reliable performance by offsetting weaknesses of individual methods. Overall, the findings highlight that methodological uncertainty in measuring slack translates directly into policy uncertainty, cautioning against exclusive reliance on any single output gap estimate.

title: Remote Work & Growing Divergence in Home Location Distributions
affiliations: University of Baltimore, Southeast University, University of Glasgow and Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology

detail.title: Remote Work & Growing Divergence in Home Location Distributions
detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic triggered a historic and rapid expansion of remote work, fundamentally reshaping where people live and how urban systems function. Although prior research has documented broad patterns of pandemic-era suburbanization and rising telework, we still lack granular and systematic evidence on how the residential spatial distributions of remote workers (RWs) and on-site workers (OWs) have diverged over time. Understanding these shifts is essential because the relative locations of RWs and OWs influence housing demand, commuting patterns, urban fiscal health, social equity, and the long-term resilience of cities. This study addresses this critical gap by using anonymized monthly residential data from the Current Population Survey to track RW and OW location patterns across U.S. counties from 2020 to 2022. By applying the Wasserstein Distance metric, we quantify the magnitude and evolution of RW-OW residential divergence, and estimate fixed-effects and multilevel models to identify structural drivers of this separation. Results reveal a gradual-and potentially lasting-increase in spatial divergence, particularly in counties with lower concentrations of knowledge workers. These findings contribute important new evidence on the spatial consequences of remote work and highlight emerging risks for geographic and social inequality, offering valuable insights for urban planning, housing policy, and regional economic development.

title: How Geopolitics Influences the Exports of Chinese Firms
affiliations: , ESCP Europe and Research Department, OFCE (French Observatory of Economic Conditions)

detail.title: How Geopolitics Influences the Exports of Chinese Firms
detail.abstract: This paper investigates how geopolitical relationships shape Chinese exports, asking whether exporters systematically favor politically aligned countries-and whether that preference holds during periods of geopolitical turbulence. Unlike most existing studies, which focus on imports or multinational enterprises (MNEs) with a Western-centric perspective, we use a high-frequency panel of over 17 million monthly firm-product-destination export transactions from Chinese Customs (2000-2006). We match this data with the Political Relationship Index (PRI) developed by Tsinghua University to analyze how changes in bilateral political relations shape trade flows. Our empirical strategy relies on a robust log-linear specification with firm-product, destination-country, month and year fixed effects, and controls for tariff variation. We test for both asymmetric and non-linear effects by interacting the PRI with indicators of extreme positive and negative geopolitical events. Our results consistently show that stronger bilateral political relations significantly increase Chinese exports. We also find evidence of asymmetric responses: exporters react more strongly to diplomatic improvements than to deteriorations. Using extreme geopolitical events, we show that positive events amplify the export response to political alignment, while negative events tend to dampen it. This pattern is especially pronounced among foreign firms and exporters of differentiated products, suggesting that political alignment plays a critical role in global value chain dynamics. In a world of growing political fragmentation, our findings underline the growing interplay between diplomacy and international trade. They reveal that friendtrading is not just a policy discourse-it is already reflected in the strategic behavior of exporters.

title: Explainable AI in U.S. Banking Fraud Detection: A Comparative Framework for Regulatory Compliance, Model Transparency, and Risk Governance

detail.title: Explainable AI in U.S. Banking Fraud Detection: A Comparative Framework for Regulatory Compliance, Model Transparency, and Risk Governance

detail.abstract: The increasing adoption of machine learning models in U.S. banking fraud detection has raised critical concerns regarding model transparency, regulatory compliance, and risk governance. While explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques have been proposed to address these challenges, financial institutions continue to face uncertainty regarding the selection, evaluation, and governance of appropriate explanation methods across diverse fraud-detection use cases. This study presents a comparative and governance-oriented framework for explainable AI in U.S. banking systems, synthesizing model-agnostic and model-specific explanation techniques commonly used in fraud analytics. Building upon prior application-focused research on interpretable transaction modeling and agebased fraud analysis, this paper shifts the focus from individual implementations to a system-level evaluation of explainability methods under regulatory and operational constraints. The proposed framework evaluates explainable AI approaches across dimensions of transparency, stability, regulatory interpretability, bias awareness, and operational risk management. The study further discusses alignment with U.S. financial regulatory expectations and outlines practical guidance for responsible model deployment in fraud-detection environments. By providing a comparative and governance-centered perspective, this paper contributes a practical reference for financial institutions, policymakers, and analytics practitioners seeking to implement explainable AI solutions that balance predictive performance with accountability and regulatory compliance in U.S. banking fraud detection.

title: The "Great Reshuffling" and Entrepreneurship
affiliations: , University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign - Department of Finance and Washington University in Saint Louis, John M. Olin Business School

detail.title: The "Great Reshuffling" and Entrepreneurship

declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge funding support from the Ewing Marion Kauffman Foundation.

detail.abstract: The recent pandemic induced a large reallocation in labor markets that coincided with a surge in entrepreneurial entry. Using the universe of U.S. administrative tax records, we study how the "Great Reshuffling" reshaped transitions into entrepreneurship, entrant characteristics, and subsequent individual and firm outcomes. We document a persistent increase in entry, with larger gains among women with children. These entrants experience higher average income but greater income volatility. Firms founded during this period exhibit higher survival and profitability though are less likely to employ workers. Our evidence points to a persistent reallocation toward smaller, owner-operated businesses rather than short-lived experimentation.

title: Affective Load as an Economic Variable: Mental Health, Regulatory Capacity, and the Hidden Costs of Institutional Design

detail.abstract: Global increases in depression, anxiety, and aggressive behavior are commonly examined within clinical, epidemiological, or sociocultural frameworks. While these approaches provide important insights, they tend to conceptualize mental health outcomes as downstream effects of individual vulnerability, life events, or access to care. This article advances a different analytical position. It conceptualizes affective states such as chronic anxiety, depressive withdrawal, and dysregulated aggression as systemic indicators of regulatory overload embedded within socioinstitutional environments. Drawing on systems psychology, regulatory theory, and macroeconomic resilience research, the paper introduces affective load as a measurable and economically consequential variable. Affective load is defined as the cumulative emotional and regulatory demand imposed on individuals by institutional complexity, procedural density, normative inconsistency, and misaligned feedback structures across education, labor, and governance systems. The central argument is that when affective load persistently exceeds the adaptive regulatory capacity of a population, mental health symptoms emerge not as isolated clinical conditions but as predictable system-level responses. These responses generate substantial economic consequences through reduced productivity, constrained innovation, labor market disengagement, increased healthcare utilization, and long-term dependency trajectories. By reframing mental health from a compensatory expenditure into a form of latent economic capital, the article proposes a shift in policy logic from treatment-centered mitigation toward anticipatory institutional design. The framework offers an integrative lens for analyzing how emotional regulation, economic performance, and governance architecture co-evolve within complex societies.

title: The Macroprudential Approach to Systemic Risk
affiliations: University of Malta - Department of Banking and Finance and Malta Financial Services Authority

detail.title: The Macroprudential Approach to Systemic Risk

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Both authors are officials of the Malta Financial Services Authority.

contentFormat.other: An article - Accepted - FSA Regulatory and Compliance Insights

detail.abstract: The Global Financial Crisis (GFC) of 2008 unequivocally exposed the fatal insufficiency of microprudential supervision, which, by focusing solely on the resilience of individual institutions, failed to prevent systemic collapse. This article argues that the subsequent global adoption of macroprudential policy (MaPP) represents a fundamental and necessary paradigm shift in financial oversight. MaPP transcends the limitations of the "fallacy of composition" by adopting a holistic, systemwide approach, targeting vulnerabilities and mitigating the build-up of systemic risk through a rigorous policy cycle and a macroprudential tools, including capital-based measures (e.g., CCyB) and borrower-based measures (e.g., LTV/DSTI ratios). While the macroprudential framework for the banking sector is mature, the system's resilience remains challenged by the non-bank financial intermediation (NBFI) sector (e.g., asset managers and insurers). The article concludes that the ongoing success of MaPP hinges on the complete integration of the NBFI sector into a cohesive, system-wide framework, which remains the critical, incomplete frontier of 21st-century financial supervision. This article is based on a lecture delivered by the authors as part of a course on financial services law at the University of Malta.

title: Which Days Matter for Global Equity Markets? Using Options to Price Events in the Global Calendar

Due to the interconnected nature of global equity markets, foreign economic developments could also matter for investors in domestic equity markets.

title: US Monetary Policy, Exchange Rates, and Delayed Portfolio Adjustments
affiliations: Yonsei University, Soongsil University and Sogang University

detail.title: US Monetary Policy, Exchange Rates, and Delayed Portfolio Adjustments
detail.abstract: What accounts for cross-country heterogeneity in exchange rate responses to U.S. monetary policy shocks? Using daily data around Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announcements, we show that countries with deeper financial markets experience larger currency depreciations following U.S. monetary tightening. This heterogeneity is substantially stronger for forward guidance shocks than for contemporaneous target rate surprises. To interpret these findings, we extend a gradual portfolio adjustment model by allowing portfolio adjustment costs to decline with financial market depth and by modeling forward guidance as a news shock to the expected future path of interest rates. In the model, deeper markets weaken effective discounting and place greater weight on expected future interest rate differentials, selectively amplifying the exchange rate response to forward guidance shocks. The model reproduces the key empirical patterns, providing a unified explanation for heterogeneous short-run exchange rate dynamics.

title: General Equilibrium Models with Heterogeneous Households: A Grid-Free Approach via Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, SKEMA Business School, Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro (PUC-Rio) and University of Auckland

detail.title: General Equilibrium Models with Heterogeneous Households: A Grid-Free Approach via Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming
detail.abstract: We develop a unified, grid-free numerical framework for heterogeneous-agent economies with incomplete markets based on Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming (SDDP). The method scales across three environments of increasing complexity. We begin with a canonical consumption-saving problem, showing how SDDP constructs nonparametric value-function approximations without state-space discretization. We then apply the approach to the Huggett and Aiyagari models, embedding SDDP within a stationaryequilibrium routine that computes market-clearing prices without Eulerequation enforcement. Finally, we extend the method to the Krusell-Smith model with aggregate risk, introducing SPHERIS, an SDDP-based algorithm that replaces parametric forecasting rules with a non-parametric HiddenMarkov representation of factor-price dynamics. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that the approach delivers accurate policies, reproduces benchmark results, and remains computationally tractable in high-dimensional settings, offering a robust alternative to traditional grid-based and parametric methods.

title: The Cyclicality of Guaranteed Financing and Investment Efficiency
affiliations: Shandong University of Finance and Economics, , Shanghai University of Finance and Economics and Southern University of Science and Technology - Department of Finance

detail.title: The Cyclicality of Guaranteed Financing and Investment Efficiency
detail.abstract: This paper develops a two-stage guarantee–investment (G–I) model to analyze how entrepreneurs adjust their financing and investment decisions in response to macroeconomic regime shifts. We study a cash-constrained entrepreneur who funds a project through a fully guaranteed bank loan and later obtains performance-contingent equity injections from the guarantor. The macroeconomy evolves according to a Markov regime-switching process, leading to regime-dependent financing choices and state-contingent investment and default thresholds. We provide closed-form solutions that demonstrate a cyclical mechanism: during recessions, rising guarantee fees encourage higher leverage and induce inefficient overinvestment. Reducing such fees through policy intervention can effectively alleviate downturn-driven resource misallocation by lowering associated default risk. Our findings highlight how coordinating loan guarantees with follow-on equity provision can ease financing constraints, offering practical insights for designing robust guarantee programs that perform well under macroeconomic risk.

title: The State of AI Competition in Advanced Economies
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.abstract: Global competition in artificial intelligence (AI) has intensified in recent years. Some assessments emphasize US exceptionalism, while others argue that China is eroding US dominance. By contrast, the progress of other advanced foreign economies (AFEs) receives far less attention.

title: The Costs of Climate Inaction and Fiscal Sustainability: An Overview of the State-of-the-Art Approaches and Estimates for the Netherlands
affiliations: , PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency and

detail.title: The Costs of Climate Inaction and Fiscal Sustainability: An Overview of the State-of-the-Art Approaches and Estimates for the Netherlands
detail.abstract: Costs of climate inaction result from a failure to implement climate mitigation and adaptation measures. These costs vary across geographies and affect diverse economic actors unevenly. Different climate risks translate into physical, direct economic, indirect economic, and financial damages. We survey leading international approaches for assessing the economic costs of climate inaction. We present the results of this overview as a 5-step methodological framework, and provide a systematic mapping of the available data for the Netherlands. We find that the majority of efforts concern scenario development, quantification of physical impacts, and their monetization into direct economic damages. In contrast, economic assessments of indirect damages for the Netherlands are scarce, typically performed as part of EU-wide analyses and focusing on a single hazard. Globally, the fiscal sustainability of governmental budgets in the face of accelerating climate risks and weak climate action raises concerns, with the first empirical evidence of declining creditworthiness due to physical climate risks. Yet, such assessments for the Netherlands are lacking. Future work should focus on the general equilibrium analysis of short-term spillover effects of compound physical climate risks, their medium/long-term macroeconomic impacts, and financial analysis of their consequences on the fiscal sustainability of the Netherlands.

title: Hyperinflation Perceptions: An Experimental Study
affiliations: , University of Southampton and University of London

detail.title: Hyperinflation Perceptions: An Experimental Study

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study has been approved by the Cyprus National Bioethics Committee (CNBC DECISION#2023.01.104).
declarations.funderStatement: This project has received funding from the European Union’s Horizon 2020 Research and innovation Programme under Grant Agreement number: [857636 (SInnoPSis), 101079196 (Twinning for Excellence in Management and Economics of Research and Innovation (TWIN4MERIT))].

detail.abstract: Consumers' perceptions of current inflation play a key role in understanding household consumption and investment decisions as well as the impact of monetary policies. Evidence from countries with low or moderate inflation shows that people's perception of inflation often diverges significantly and systematically from official inflation rates. We examine the relationship between actual and perceived inflation in a hyperinflation environment, and compare it to the corresponding relationships in low and moderate inflation regimes. Our experimental results show that, opposite to low inflation, hyperinflation is greatly underestimated in people's perceptions. Moreover, the accuracy of inflation perceptions, as inflation rises, exhibits an inverse-U shape, which confirms our novel, preregistered "Perception Accuracy Inversion" hypothesis.

title: Organization Capital, Bond Issuance Spread, and Debt Financing Choices
affiliations: University of Sussex , Fordham University  , The University of Sydney - Discipline of Finance and University of Sussex

detail.title: Organization Capital, Bond Issuance Spread, and Debt Financing Choices
detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between firm-level organization capital and corporate bond issuance spreads. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in firm-level organization capital is associated with an 11.74% increase in corporate bond issuance yield spreads, consistent with organization capital elevating risk. The effect remains robust after addressing endogeneity and is stronger for firms with a higher risk of key talent leaving. We further find that firms with higher organization capital rely more on bank loans than on public bonds likely because bank financing is cheaper. Moreover, they choose shorter debt maturities, issue more short-term debt, and maintain higher leverage. The evidence highlights the central role of organization capital in shaping firms' cost of issuing public debt and financing choices.

title: Machine Learning and Technical Analysis in International Market
affiliations: Victoria University of Wellington

detail.title: Machine Learning and Technical Analysis in International Market
detail.abstract: This chapter explores the use of various machine learning models to forecast stock returns in the international market . We calculate 107 technical variables and use them to train an array of machine learning models. Using data from 25 markets, we uncover machine learning's superior performance over OLS (our benchmark model) in predicting future stock returns, in terms of both prediction accuracy and economic gains. We also show that machine learning generates superior performance among big, liquid firms and adds value during periods of downward market trend. The international heterogeneity in machine learning outperformance is associated with market features such as macroeconomic fundamentals, cultural traits, and the information environment.

detail.abstract: Capital allocation in biotechnology often relies on success benchmarks that do not fully account for incomplete outcome information in observed program data. We apply proprietary modeling to a universe of 384,846 drug development programs identified from public clinical trial registries. We analyze a subset of programs constructed from public records using proprietary selection procedures; details withheld. Applying a proprietary classification procedure (details withheld), we find that the vast majority of eligible programs do not satisfy the proprietary assessment. Programs without explicit discontinuation evidence are treated as having unknown outcomes rather than assumed failed. This public draft intentionally omits proprietary parameterization; not intended to enable replication.

title: Commitment Without Binding: Why Institutional Promises Fail

detail.title: Commitment Without Binding: Why Institutional Promises Fail

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Institutions routinely make commitments-to reform, sustainability, safety, equity, or resilience-yet fail to execute them even when intent is sincere, legitimacy is high, and learning mechanisms are present. This paper advances a structural explanation: institutional commitments are not architected to bind future action. Contemporary governance systems rely on promises, targets, and declarations that lack enforceability across time, authority boundaries, and decision cycles, producing systematic divergence between commitment and execution.

title: (Benelux') Friends in Need: EU Council Voting Alignment Analysis
affiliations: Department of North European and Baltic languages, MGIMO (Moscow State University of International Relations)

detail.title: (Benelux') Friends in Need: EU Council Voting Alignment Analysis
detail.abstract: Since the mid-20th century, the strategic foreign policy approaches of the Netherlands, Belgium, and Luxembourg have been similar, consisting in active participation in European integration and a rejection of neutrality in favor of reliance on the United States and NATO. Since the late 1980s, signs of diverging paths emerged: Belgium and Luxembourg advocate deeper European integration, orienting toward France and Germany, while the Netherlands shows "greater reluctance and ambivalence" due to EU expansion and becoming a net contributor, unlike net-recipient Belgium and Luxembourg. Dutch concerns over budget drains fueled caution on enlargements (2004, 2007, 2013), rejection of the EU-Ukraine Association Agreement, and the 2005 EU Constitution referendum. Crises strengthened Euroscepticism, prompting alliances like the Frugal Four and Hanseatic League 2.0. Council voting confirms patterns: Netherlands aligns with Nordics, Baltics, Austria, and previously UK; Belgium and Luxembourg-with Southern Europe, France and Germany, while diverging from the majority on economic, agriculture, and fisheries issues.

title: Business Cycles and Earnings Inequality
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Business Cycles and Earnings Inequality

declarations.funderStatement: Support from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Grant No. R9213) is gratefully acknowledged.

detail.abstract: I construct a quarterly measure of earnings inequality and document the following facts. First, productivity and government expenditure shocks significantly affect earnings inequality, while monetary policy shocks have small effects. Second, unanticipated innovations in earnings inequality, summarizing redistributive forces from the bottom to the top, substantially decrease aggregate demand in an inverted hump-shaped manner. Finally, the power of stabilization policies increases with the level of inequality. These empirical results are rationalized by a tractable two-agent model featuring a cyclical extensive margin of being credit-constrained, decreasing relative risk aversion preferences, and a financial income accruing to the credit-constrained agents.

title: Macroeconomic Belief Distortions and Expected Returns in Treasury Bonds
affiliations: SILC Business School, Shanghai University, University of Texas at Dallas - Jindal School of Management and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Macroeconomic Belief Distortions and Expected Returns in Treasury Bonds

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No
declarations.funderStatement: We thank the financial support from the National Social Science Foundation of China (No. 25&ZD132) by Xiaoneng Zhu.

detail.abstract: We demonstrate that systematic belief distortions arising from heterogeneous expectations are first-order drivers of bond risk premia. Utilizing partial least squares on a high-dimensional panel of real-time macroeconomic indicators, we construct a bond expected-return factor that avoids look-ahead bias. The constructed factor tracks a broad array of expectation errors, including ex ante macroeconomic distortions, subjective risk premiums, and monetary policy surprises, and provides strong in-sample and out-of-sample predictive power for bond excess returns, beyond yield curve factors and other known bond-return predictors. These findings highlight that belief bias and disagreement jointly shape bond expected returns, unspanned by the yield curve.

title: Borders Bear the Brunt: State Environmental Review and Severed Agglomerations
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Smeal College of Business , University of Oklahoma - Michael F. Price College of Business and Monash University

detail.title: Borders Bear the Brunt: State Environmental Review and Severed Agglomerations
detail.abstract: We study how state environmental review laws (SEPAs) shape local business activity. Using a stacked, border-pair event design around staggered SEPAs, we compare adjacent counties on either side of state lines. SEPA-side border counties experience slower post-adoption growth that cumulates into persistent level losses over two decades, with no mirror-image gains across the border and no broad underperformance in state interiors. Effects are strongest for SEPA-treated counties that border large metro areas, when SEPAs have substantive provisions, and when states devote more resources to environmental protection, and they fall disproportionately on pollution-intensive sectors and small firms. In sum, local environmental regulations can erode local agglomerations, adversely affecting local small business growth.

title: To Find Relative Earnings Gains After the China Shock, Look Upstream and Outside Manufacturing
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System,  and Government of the United States of America - Bureau of the Census

detail.title: To Find Relative Earnings Gains After the China Shock, Look Upstream and Outside Manufacturing

publicationDetails.journalName: Board of Governors: International Finance Discussion Papers (Topic)

detail.abstract: We find that US workers outside manufacturing exhibit relative earnings increases after US trade liberalization with China. These relative gains cumulate over time as the beneficial effect of a workerâ  s upstream exposureâ  increased competition from China in input marketsâ  more than offsets the detrimental impact of her own and downstream (customer) exposures. These relative gains are smaller for non-manufacturing workers with less ex ante firm tenure and lower initial earnings, and are absent among manufacturing workers due to a lack of upstream gains and stronger downstream losses.

title: Structural Fiscalistics in Taxation: The 4-3-3-2 Grammar as an Executable Institutional Syntax Reframing Canadian and International Tax Law as a Routing System

detail.title: Structural Fiscalistics in Taxation: The 4-3-3-2 Grammar as an Executable Institutional Syntax Reframing Canadian and International Tax Law as a Routing System
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces Structural Fiscalistics as an evidence-to-structure framework for reading tax law as an executable routing system rather than a rulebook of accumulating provisions. In complex files, difficulty rarely arises from the absence of rules; it arises because the same economic event can be routed into materially different institutional outcomes depending on how it is classified, attributed, and timed across decision nodes—an instability amplified by cross-border interfaces.

The paper fixes a procedural order—Evidence → Structure → Readout—by coupling Fiscal Epistemology (FE), which restricts inputs to traceable, admissible records, with Fiscal Geometry (FG), which renders those inputs into auditable structural objects. This non-reversal pipeline prevents downstream reasoning from substituting narrative plausibility for accountable evidence.

Within this method, the paper formalizes the 4-3-3-2 grammar as the minimal executable syntax of Canadian tax law: four income rails (employment, business, property, capital); three tax subjects (T1 individual, T2 corporation, T3 trust); three conversion modes (timing, type, taxpayer); and two structural triggers (title change, use change) that connect tax routing to commercial, corporate, and property law. Domestic and international tax are shown to operate under the same grammar, with cross-border regimes intensifying the frequency of these conversions at jurisdictional boundaries.

The contribution is methodological rather than doctrinal. By converting tax analysis from section-by-section interpretation into reproducible routing representations, the framework enables consistent case comparability, structured cross-border synthesis, and audit-ready outputs. Taxation emerges as a primary domain for executable institutional modeling in practice workflows and AI-mediated compliance systems.
