title: Earnings Manipulation Under Pressure: How Financial Covenants Shape Reporting Behavior and Risk

detail.title: Earnings Manipulation Under Pressure: How Financial Covenants Shape Reporting Behavior and Risk
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between financial constraints from covenants, measured through a novel Financial Covenant Pressure Index (FCPI), and anticipatory firm behavior in earnings manipulation. I construct the FCPI by applying large language models (LLMs) to corporate disclosures to develop a forward-looking text-based measure of financial constraints that is accurate and scalable. Using mixed-effects logistic regression models on a sample of U.S. non-financial firms, I find that heightened financial constraints significantly increase the likelihood of earnings misstatements. Firms subject to tighter financial constraints proactively manipulate reported earnings to avoid triggering violations even before any formal breach occurs. Larger firms, those with elevated leverage, and those with a history of high FCPI exhibit the strongest misstatement reactions, implying an amplification by financing stress. This study extends the covenant literature by documenting how financial constraints shape managerial decisions in advance of any violation. The findings offer important insights for regulators, lenders, and investors, highlighting the need to monitor firms under financial constraints and the broader implications of financial constraints for corporate governance and risk management.

title: Words of Conviction: Using AI to Map Confidence in Corporate Communication

detail.title: Words of Conviction: Using AI to Map Confidence in Corporate Communication
detail.abstract: This paper develops a natural language processing framework to measure executive overconfidence in earnings calls and examine its effects on firm outcomes. Using prompt-based inference with large language models, I classify linguistic expressions of confidence along three psychological dimensions: overestimation, overplacement, and overprecision. The measure aligns with traditional behavioral proxies and captures both persistent individual traits and time-varying managerial tone. Firms led by more confident CEOs trade at lower valuation multiples and exhibit greater firm risk, as reflected in higher return and accounting-based volatility. A one-point increase in the overconfidence score (on the 1-4 scale) corresponds to a 6-12% lower Tobin's Q, a 6-20% increase in volatility, and modestly higher investment, leverage, and acquisition activity. These effects are stronger among smaller, less profitable, and less tangible firms, consistent with greater managerial discretion. Text-based confidence thus provides an economically meaningful behavioral signal that helps explain systematic variation in corporate valuation, risk, and financial policies.

title: Artificial Code

detail.title: Artificial Code

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: BYU Law School

detail.abstract:
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly transformed software development, enabling the production of high-quality code at unprecedented speed and scale. Yet despite widespread litigation over the use of copyrighted works to train AI systems in fields such as music, journalism, and visual art, the software industry has thus far remained largely absent from the AI copyright wars. The explanation lies in the pervasiveness of free and open source software (FOSS), which has provided AI developers with a vast, low-risk corpus of training material while simultaneously insulating them from copyright liability. Ironically, however, the same AI technologies that have benefited from the FOSS ecosystem now threaten to undermine its legal and normative foundations.

The core issue, this Article contends, is that much AI-generated software-what this Article terms "artificial code"-is not eligible for copyright protection under prevailing U.S. law. Because copyright requires human authorship, artificial code often falls into the public domain, rendering traditional copyright-based FOSS licensing frameworks increasingly ineffective. As copyright recedes as a viable governance mechanism, software innovators are likely to turn instead to trade secrecy and patents to protect their software innovations. These alternative regimes, while legally robust, are often at odds with the openness, reciprocity, and collaborative norms that have long defined the modern software economy.

This shift has profound implications. As more software is withheld from public access or encumbered by exclusionary patent rights, the software commons risks contraction. In turn, the contraction of that commons threatens the future development of AI systems themselves. Generative models depend on continued access to large volumes of humancurated software to avoid degradation and "model collapse," as well as inventive AI innovations. If the FOSS ecosystem erodes, AI systems may find themselves deprived of the very inputs necessary to sustain their progress.

By tracing the historical rise of FOSS, diagnosing the legal vulnerabilities introduced by artificial code, and examining the growing pull of alternative intellectual property regimes, this Article highlights a paradox at the heart of modern AI development: generative AI may be sowing the seeds of its own stagnation. The Article concludes by exploring how these concerns may arise in other creative contexts, too, as well as assessing possible responses aimed at preserving openness in software and AI innovation while accommodating the realities of AI-generated code.

title: Tariff-Risk Disclosure in 10-Ks and Stock Market Responses to the Liberation Day shock
affiliations: Cyprus University of Technology, ,  and Cyprus University of Technology

detail.title: Tariff-Risk Disclosure in 10-Ks and Stock Market Responses to the Liberation Day shock
detail.abstract: This study investigates how firms' recognition of tariff-related risk in (pre-shock) 10-K disclosures affects stock-market reactions to the April 2, 2025, "Liberation Day" tariff shock. We use a machine-learning approach to identify semantically meaningful tariffrisk recognition across the entire 10-K filing, with separate analyses for Risk Factors ("Item 1A") and the remaining sections of the filing, excluding Item 1A ("Other"). Our results show that firms that explicitly acknowledge tariff risk experience significantly lower abnormal returns around the announcement. Interestingly, this effect is not driven by disclosures in the Item 1A section, but instead arises from tariff-risk recognition in the Other sections of the 10-K and is concentrated among firms facing high litigation risk. The findings highlight the informational role of narrative risk recognition and the importance of where such disclosures appear within corporate filings.

title: The Dual Nature of Social Media: Information Frictions, Attention Externalities, and Market Efficiency in the Digital Economy
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Dual Nature of Social Media: Information Frictions, Attention Externalities, and Market Efficiency in the Digital Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: The proliferation of social media platforms has fundamentally reshaped the landscape of modern economics, creating a complex ecosystem where information dissemination, labor productivity, and consumer welfare intersect. This research paper provides an exhaustive economic analysis of social media's impact on market dynamics, focusing on the trade-off between reduced information asymmetry and increased attention externalities. Drawing upon a synthesis of fifteen seminal papers published between 2020 and 2025, we investigate how algorithmic curation and digital advertising auctions influence consumer decision-making and market prices. Our methodology combines a comprehensive systematic literature review with a proposed structural time-allocation model that accounts for the shadow price of attention. We find that while social media significantly lowers search costs and enhances market matching efficiency-particularly in financial and product markets-these gains are frequently offset by negative externalities such as mental health deterioration, political polarization, and reduced labor efficiency due to cognitive fragmentation. Specifically, our analysis suggests that the welfare effects of social media follow an inverted-U shape, where initial adoption drives surplus through connectivity, but excessive consumption leads to diminishing returns driven by the 'attention tax' imposed by platform design. The paper concludes with policy implications, arguing that current antitrust and privacy regulations (like GDPR) may be insufficient without addressing the core economic incentives of the attention economy, proposing instead a framework of 'algorithmic accountability' and taxation on excessive data extraction.

title:
Structural Convexity Index
Capturing Flight-to-Quality with an Always-on Long/Short Crisis Strategy

detail.title:
Structural Convexity Index
Capturing Flight-to-Quality with an Always-on Long/Short Crisis Strategy
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Structural Convexity Index (SCI), a systematic long/short strategy engineered to deliver crisis alpha during material equity drawdowns while maintaining positive long-term drift. Unlike defensive approaches that depend on timing signals or market path-such as trend-following and volatility trading-SCI is "alwayson," seeking immediate responsiveness in fast, V-shaped declines by holding permanent durable-minus-fragile spreads. The strategy targets a single, persistent mechanismflight-to-quality-expressed across three uncorrelated sectors through factor-aligned pairs: Gold (long physical gold via GLD; short junior miners via GDXJ), Energy (long integrated majors via XLE; short oilfield services via IEZ), and Credit (long intermediate U.S. Treasuries via IEI; short mortgage REITs via REM). SCI is constructed at 200% long and 100% short (100% net long) and is rebalanced monthly to maintain fixed exposures. Over the 2007-2025 simulation period, SCI generated a hypothetical 7.8% CAGR with-84% downside capture relative to the S&P 500. The strategy simulated positive returns in every major equity drawdown exceeding 15%, including a hypothetical +24.2% return during the 2022 inflation shock when stock-bond diversification failed. These results suggest SCI's convexity is regime-independent, rooted in structural fragility and liquidity-driven repricing rather than falling interest rates. Finally, we argue the strategy's persistence is supported by a behavioral moat: benchmark-constrained capital struggles to tolerate the tracking error inherent in structural crisis protection. SCI is a benchmark index for research and measurement purposes only and cannot be invested in directly. Any implementation would require an investment vehicle, the performance of which would differ from the index due to fees, financing/borrow costs, taxes, execution frictions, and operational constraints. Research updates are published at RheonResearch.com.

title: Temporal granularity, settlement frequency, and the economic structure of tail risk in electricity prices
affiliations: Gdańsk University of Technology and Gdańsk University of Technology

detail.title: Temporal granularity, settlement frequency, and the economic structure of tail risk in electricity prices
detail.abstract: This paper examines how higher temporal granularity reshapes the economic nature of tail risk in electricity prices. Using high-frequency data from the Polish day-ahead market, we compare price returns observed at the 15-minute resolution with an hourly benchmark constructed from the same underlying quarter-hourly clearing prices. The analysis deliberately focuses on distribution-based tail-risk measures rather than volatility dynamics or structural price-formation models.Contrary to the common presumption that finer settlement intervals mechanically amplify extreme price movements, we find no systematic increase in tail magnitude as captured by extreme quantiles. Instead, higher temporal granularity primarily reallocates tail risk from magnitude to intensity: extreme price changes occur more frequently and in a more temporally concentrated manner, while their typical scale remains broadly unchanged. Excess kurtosis and exceedance-based diagnostics consistently indicate stronger tail concentration and higher exceedance intensity under the 15-minute resolution once differences in sampling frequency are accounted for.These findings suggest that price risk in electricity markets cannot be treated as a one-dimensional object. Settlement frequency shapes not only how tail risk is measured, but how it materialises economically, shifting exposure from rare, event-driven extremes toward persistent, process-driven price impulses. This distinction is relevant for risk measurement, liquidity management, and the design of market time units in day-ahead electricity markets, where settlement conventions directly condition the timing and frequency of cash-flow exposure.

title: Forecasting the Oil and Gas Industry Equities: A t-LASSO Approach
affiliations: University of North Carolina at Wilmington

detail.title: Forecasting the Oil and Gas Industry Equities: A t-LASSO Approach
detail.abstract: We investigate predictability of the equity risk premium for the oil and gas industry by using LASSO regressions with non-Gaussian errors to account for extreme observations. We utilize predictors developed by the oil price forecasting literature and consider their moving averages to proxy economic trends. We show that the constructed model has statistically and economically significant predictive power for oil and gas stocks, and the trend of the world industrial production index is the most important predictor. This conclusion is robust to a battery of checks.

title: Demand for Ethanol considering Spatially Differentiated Fuel Retailers
affiliations: International Monetary Fund (IMF)

detail.title: Demand for Ethanol considering Spatially Differentiated Fuel Retailers
detail.abstract: Consumer choice in fuel markets is central to understanding competition, environmental policy, and energy transition. In Brazil, one of the world’s largest producers and consumers of ethanol, fuel retailers face an environment where consumers can substitute between traditional gasoline and renewable ethanol. The coexistence of these two fuel types presents a natural laboratory for analyzing substitution patterns, pricing strategies, and the role of market size in shaping demand. From a methodological perspective, the study of such markets requires econometric models capable of capturing correlated preferences and heterogeneity across fuel alternatives. The adoption of novel vehicle and fuel technologies is characterized by heterogeneous consumer preferences, where demand is mediated by relative price, perceived utility, and behavioral factors. Even with the widespread availability of flex-fuel vehicles (FFVs), consumer fuel choice is governed by a constrained utility maximization framework that incorporates not only comparative fuel prices and energy content but also spatial frictions (e.g., retailer proximity), search costs, and non-pecuniary attributes. Empirical evidence suggests that retailer network density and localized price differentials significantly influence switching behavior between gasoline and ethanol.

title: Modeling Optimal Incentives for the Electric Vehicle Market
affiliations: The University of Manchester and Corvinus University of Budapest

detail.title: Modeling Optimal Incentives for the Electric Vehicle Market
detail.abstract: Governments face increasing pressure to meet net zero targets, requiring the rapid electrification of transport and heating. This paper studies how public incentives can be designed and timed to support the transition from internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles to electric vehicles (EVs) in a fiscally sustainable way.We combine cross-country data on vehicle prices, subsidies, and charging infrastructure with a dynamic policy evaluation framework. Using the United Kingdom as a representative case study, we model EV adoption as a function of economic conditions and government incentives under uncertainty. The framework allows us to compare alternative incentive pathways and quantify their long-run fiscal and environmental implications.Our results highlight a fundamental trade-off between early and delayed intervention. Policies based on sales penalties tend to induce early and gradual deployment of incentives, whereas terminal targets alone create incentives for governments to postpone action. Delayed intervention, however, leads to sharp late-stage subsidy requirements and may generate congestion effects in public spending and infrastructure. The model therefore provides a data-driven tool for evaluating the timing of EV incentive policies and identifying transition pathways that avoid excessive fiscal and implementation risks.

reference: Cardozo Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-01; 103 Wash. U. L. Rev. Online (Forthcoming)
title: Property Rights v. Taxpayer Rights: The Battle Over Tax Foreclosures
affiliations: Yeshiva University - Benjamin N. Cardozo School of Law

detail.title: Property Rights v. Taxpayer Rights: The Battle Over Tax Foreclosures

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cardozo Legal Studies Research Paper No. 2026-01
publicationDetails.journalName: Cardozo Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In Tyler v. Hennepin County, the Supreme Court held that the constitution’s takings clause entitles a defaulting taxpayer to surplus proceeds generated by a tax foreclosure sale. In Pung v. Isabella County, the Court will consider whether the takings clause entitles the defaulting taxpayer to the fair market value of the foreclosed property, even if the foreclosure sale never generated that value for the municipality. Awarding the defaulting owner compensation based on fair market value would jeopardize municipal efforts to collect property taxes -- with adverse consequences for those property owners who do pay their taxes on time.

title: Challenges to Prospect Theory: Three Classes of Boundary Conditions
affiliations: Technion-Israel Institute of Technology - William Davidson Faculty of Industrial Engineering & Management

detail.title: Challenges to Prospect Theory: Three Classes of Boundary Conditions
detail.abstract: The experimental findings that motivated prospect theory reveal systematic deviations from the predictions of expected utility theory, which can be elegantly accounted for by assuming several key behavioral tendencies. However, the conditions under which these tendencies accurately capture behavior exhibit clear and important boundaries. In some cases, behavior outside these boundaries reflects biases that run in the opposite direction. This chapter reviews research that identifies, clarifies, and explains these boundary conditions. The discussion highlights three primary sources of such boundaries: the description-experience gap, presentation effects, and the impact of differing payoff distributions. The chapter also examines three classes of explanations for these phenomena: situation-specific parameters, additional behavioral tendencies not encompassed by prospect theory, and the "doubting decision maker" account. Identifying and understanding these boundary conditions-and the mechanisms that produce them-constitute a central challenge for researchers employing prospect theory.

reference: Peterson Institute for International Economics Policy Brief 26-3
title: The COVID Era Inflation Surge: Causes, Consequences, and Policy Lessons
affiliations: Harvard University and Peterson Institute for International Economics

detail.title: The COVID Era Inflation Surge: Causes, Consequences, and Policy Lessons

declarations.funderStatement: PIIE gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Smith Richardson Foundation for the research presented in this Policy Brief. The research was conducted independently; funders are not given the right to review a publication before its release.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Peterson Institute for International Economics Policy Brief 26-3
publicationDetails.journalName: Peterson Institute for International Economics (PIIE) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The COVID era inflation surge was shaped by an unusual confluence of shocks and policy responses. It nonetheless raises enduring questions about the interaction of demand, supply, expectations, and policy frameworks that decision-makers are likely to confront again. In this Policy Brief, Dynan and Wilcox distill lessons from a broad body of work produced as part of the Peterson Institute for International Economics' Understanding the COVID Era Inflation project, which brought together an extensive group of experts to examine the different facets of the inflation surge. Dynan and Wilcox synthesize the group's insights to recount the origin of the surge, evaluate the key causes and consequences, discuss the limits and strengths of policy tools, and offer lessons for policymakers to deal with future undesirable increases in inflation.

Key Takeaways:

Inflation surged globally, but its specific underlying drivers differed across economies, with implications for policy.

In the United States, excess demand combined with inelastic supply to generate the inflation surge.
On the fiscal side, the difficulty of identifying real-time capacity constraints strengthens the case for greater reliance on automatic stabilizers.

On the monetary side, in contrast, policy flexibility is especially critical in environments when uncertainty is elevated, and forecasting errors are likely.

title: Compute, Complexity, and the Scaling Laws of Return Predictability
affiliations: UCSD  and University of California, San Diego (UCSD), Rady School of Management, Students

detail.title: Compute, Complexity, and the Scaling Laws of Return Predictability
detail.abstract: Investors' computing power ("compute") governs how much signal they can extract from high-dimensional data. Drawing on insights from LLM training, we show that forecast performance follows scaling laws—stable power-law functions between accuracy and training compute—that pin down both an irreducible bound on return predictability and the rate at which extra compute closes the gap. In firm-level cross-sectional return prediction, scaling laws explain over 80% of performance variation across models. Treating compute as a primitive yields sharp economic implications: scaling laws quantify predictability limits and the value of new data, they distinguish problems with strong versus weak returns to scale, and they deliver a market-efficiency metric by mapping computational advantage into a certainty equivalent. Measured this way, computational superiority earns sizable rents: a 25% marginal increase in compute would have raised an investor’s Sharpe ratio by about 10% over the last 30 years, indicating substantial returns to computational sophistication.

title: Pandemic-Induced Housing Price Shocks and Local Government Finances: Evidence from New York School Districts

detail.title: Pandemic-Induced Housing Price Shocks and Local Government Finances: Evidence from New York School Districts

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available administrative and secondary data and does not involve human subjects. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how COVID-19-induced housing price shocks reshaped local government finances in the United States. Using school district-level data from New York State spanning 2006-2022, I apply a difference-indifferences and event-study framework to estimate the fiscal effects of pandemic-driven changes in housing prices. The results show a significant increase in property tax revenues following the COVID-19 housing price shock, driven primarily by school districts located at an intermediate distance from major city centers. Overall expenditures do not increase significantly in the short run; however, spending on debt service, employee benefits, and general government functions rises modestly. These findings highlight how pandemic-induced suburbanization translated into uneven fiscal gains across local governments and show that housing market shocks affect not only revenue levels but also the composition of public spending.

title: Policy Effort to meet Ratcheted Ambitions : The case of Utility-Scale Solar in India
affiliations: , Chalmers University of Technology - Division of Physical Resource Theory, Chalmers University of Technology and Central European University

detail.title: Policy Effort to meet Ratcheted Ambitions : The case of Utility-Scale Solar in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interest
declarations.funderStatement: SB received support from the PhD scholarship and supplementary grants from the Central European University. JJ, and LN received support from the MANIFEST project (no. 950408) funded by the European Commission’s Horizon 2020 ERC Starting Grant. JJ and AC received support from the MISTRA Electrification research programme funded by the Swedish Foundation for Strategic Environmental Research (MISTRA). AC also received support from the NEWSTEPS project funded by the Swedish Energy Agency.

detail.abstract: Accelerating the low-carbon energy transition will require rapid deployment of renewable energy technologies, especially in developing countries where energy demand is growing fast. How much of this acceleration can be left to markets, and how much must be driven by policies? On the one hand developing countries can benefit from technology learning and cost declines from the technological pioneers. On the other hand, developing countries typically pose higher risks to investors. In this paper, we argue that understanding the relative role of markets and policies in accelerating renewable energy growth in the future requires looking at how that growth has unfolded in the past. We examine the case of utilityscale solar in India, which has experienced sustained acceleration over the past decade, underpinned by rising political ambition, and favourable market conditions, including sharply falling technology costs, high solar irradiation, growing demand, and benefits from technological and policy learning from solar PV pioneers. We analyse national energy transitions as shaped by the co-evolution of technological innovation, economic development, and policy change, and map India's solar trajectory by diagnosing technological growth phases, cost trends, and policy evolution at both federal and state levels. We address four questions: (i) What is the relative role of cost decline and policy effort in driving solar growth? (ii) How do policies evolve in response to increasing deployment and declining costs? (iii) What barriers emerge at different phases of technology growth in a developing, technology-recipient country? (iv) Do later adopting regions catch up, or do disparities in deployment persist or increase over time? Our findings show that even in a highly favourable market, utility-scale solar in India has been and remains fundamentally policy-driven. As costs declined, more numerous-and more diverse-policies were required to sustain solar PV growth. Policy interventions were often triggered by emergent barriers, and growth pulses coincided with such adjustments. Many barriers mirrored those in developed countries, but emerged at different, often earlier stages, thereby signaling the need for greater policy effort in developing countries and undermining the argument for easy 'leapfrogging'. Finally, solar growth across Indian states has been and continues to be spatially uneven, with no evidence of convergence between earlier and later adopters. Instead, the co-evolution of cost, technology, and policy appears to reinforce the spatial divergence. For policymakers and researchers modelling climate mitigation pathways and seeking to understand the real-world effort needed to accelerate renewable energy deployment, our findings offer a grounded sense of what it may take. Even under favourable market conditions, sustained growth requires persistent, adaptive, and often increasingly intense policy effort.

title: Modeling Coastal Aquifer Recovery Trajectories Under Post-Conflict Intervention Scenarios: The Gaza Groundwater Crisis

detail.title: Modeling Coastal Aquifer Recovery Trajectories Under Post-Conflict Intervention Scenarios: The Gaza Groundwater Crisis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Author has no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval granted.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded research through ICL Institute

detail.abstract:
The Gaza coastal aquifer, serving as the sole natural freshwater source for approximately 2.3 million inhabitants, has experienced catastrophic degradation following decades of chronic overextraction and the acute impacts of the 2023-2025 conflict. With 97% of groundwater already unfit for human consumption prior to the conflict and approximately 80% of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure subsequently destroyed, the aquifer's long-term viability is critically uncertain. This dissertation developed spatially-explicit groundwater models to project aquifer recovery trajectories under alternative post-conflict intervention scenarios, addressing a critical gap in reconstruction planning. The research employed MODFLOW-2005 integrated with SEAWAT for variable-density flow simulation, calibrated to 30 years of historical observations (1990-2020) and validated against independent pre-conflict data (2020-2023). Model calibration achieved Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency values exceeding 0.80 for both hydraulic head (NSE = 0.86) and chloride concentration (NSE = 0.81). Results revealed current aquifer conditions of extreme degradation, with average water levels at -11.4 m below mean sea level and mean chloride concentration of 2,847 mg/L—exceeding WHO drinking water guidelines by more than an order of magnitude. Twelve intervention scenarios were simulated over a 25-year projection period. Baseline projections (no intervention) indicated continued catastrophic deterioration, with only 1.1% of the aquifer meeting WHO standards by 2050. Maximum integrated intervention combining wastewater treatment, managed aquifer recharge, desalination expansion, and demand management achieved 58.2% recovery at an estimated investment of $2.4 billion. The research identified critical threshold conditions (chloride >10,000 mg/L, water level <-15 m MSL) beyond which recovery becomes technically infeasible, with 12% of the aquifer currently exceeding these thresholds. Findings support the prioritization of wastewater treatment restoration as the highest-impact early intervention, demonstrating superior cost-effectiveness compared to desalination-focused approaches.

Keywords: groundwater modeling, coastal aquifer, seawater intrusion, post-conflict reconstruction, Gaza, WASH, water security

title: Archaeobytology: The Discipline of the Ancient Byte, A Foundational Paper on Digital Ontology, Taxonomy, and Applied Stewardship
affiliations: and Vassar College

detail.title: Archaeobytology: The Discipline of the Ancient Byte, A Foundational Paper on Digital Ontology, Taxonomy, and Applied Stewardship

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Digital preservation faces an ontological crisis: practitioners excavate the "digital dust" of the web's history without a unified theory defining the nature of the artifacts they recover. While adjacent fields like media archaeology and forensic materialism provide critical lenses for analysis, they lack a generative methodology for applying historical lessons to contemporary technical stewardship. This paper creates the discipline of Archaeobytology to fill this intellectual void. The paper establishes the Archaeobyte as the fundamental unit of inquiry, distinguishing between tangible files and conceptual "ghosts" of past interfaces. It introduces The Triage, a state-based taxonomy classifying artifacts not by format, but by their functional relationship to the current ecosystem: the Vivibyte (living usage), Umbrabyte (broken context), Petribyte (fossilized function), and Nullibyte (lost). Finally, it articulates the Archive & Anvil methodology, a synthesis of scholarly excavation and critical making. This framework redefines the practitioner as an Archaeobytologist-a "scholar-smith" who studies the digital past to forge sovereign, resilient frameworks for the future. This work serves as the foundational declaration for the discipline, inviting scholars to move beyond nostalgia and engage in applied digital stewardship.

title: Content Moderation and Antitrust: Part VI -Is there an Empty Set at the Intersection of Antitrust and Content Moderation?
affiliations: International Center for Law & Economics  and International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE)

detail.title: Content Moderation and Antitrust: Part VI -Is there an Empty Set at the Intersection of Antitrust and Content Moderation?

declarations.funderStatement: No specific funding for this project.

detail.abstract: Antitrust scrutiny of large technology platforms has continued apace in ways both more and less familiar under the second Trump administration and its antitrust agencies. Of some controversy is enforcers' interest in a novel area of inquiry; that is, whether-and under what conditions-content moderation might prove anticompetitive, in violation of the antitrust laws. That question raises another: if so, would enforcement of the antitrust laws against such content moderation run afoul of the speech clause of the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution? We suggest a qualified "no" as an answer to the first question and a likely "yes" as an answer to the second. While one might, in the abstract, imagine an antitrust case against something like a tech platform's content moderation practices, we suspect that finding facts and circumstances to make out a convincing antitrust case involving the actual tech platforms of interest would prove tough sledding. Moreover, recent Supreme Court precedent suggests limits to the reach of antitrust, at least as pertains to content moderation by privately operated tech platforms.

title: Spatial Misallocation in Education: The Left-Behind and Land Reforms in China
affiliations: Kobe University - Graduate School of Economics, Peking University HSBC Business School and Peking University HSBC Business School

detail.title: Spatial Misallocation in Education: The Left-Behind and Land Reforms in China
detail.abstract: At the beginning of the 2000s, China introduced major agricultural land rights reforms. We study how these reforms shape family migration and the human capital accumulation of rural-origin children when education quality differs sharply between rural and urban areas. Exploiting staggered provincial adoption, we show that (i) strengthened land security reduces by 33% the likelihood that migrant workers leave children behind in rural areas, and (ii) each additional childhood year that rural-born children spend in urban areas increases the probability of university enrollment by about 1 percentage point. We then interpret these effects and quantify long-run implications in a calibrated heterogeneous-agent model with incomplete markets, migration, and education choices. Moving to fully secure land property rights generates a 2.1% consumption-equivalent welfare gain by reallocating talent and reducing precautionary distortions in migration and savings. We demonstrate that general equilibrium adjustments in land markets play a first-order role for the aggregate and distributional evaluation of the reform.

title: Living Within the Lie? Geoeconomics, Economic Power, and the Structural Rupture of the Liberal Order

detail.title: Living Within the Lie? Geoeconomics, Economic Power, and the Structural Rupture of the Liberal Order
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the contemporary international system is no longer undergoing a gradual transition but rather a structural rupture in which economic integration has been reprogrammed as an instrument of power. Under the emerging geoeconomic paradigm, trade, finance, technology, and regulatory frameworks are increasingly mobilized as tools of economic coercion, reshaping the functional role of international law and institutions. The traditional narrative of a rules-based international order persists rhetorically, yet operates in practice through asymmetric enforcement, selective compliance, and strategic flexibility. This dissonance generates systemic risks for states and firms alike, particularly for middle powers lacking sufficient market size or coercive capacity to negotiate bilaterally with hegemonic actors. By integrating Law & Economics, International Political Economy, and institutional analysis, this paper examines how legal norms, regulatory mechanisms, and compliance architectures are transformed from constraints on power into infrastructure for its exercise. The analysis highlights diversification, institutional coordination, and domestic economic resilience as central strategies for mitigating geoeconomic vulnerability. Ultimately, the paper contends that naming the reality of economic coercion is a prerequisite for restoring coherence between law, power, and governance in a fragmented global order.

title: Debt Imperialism: From Financial Hegemony to the Chaos of Semi-Peripheries
affiliations: and University of Milan

detail.title: Debt Imperialism: From Financial Hegemony to the Chaos of Semi-Peripheries
detail.abstract: This paper argues that the current proliferation of commercial tensions, monetary conflicts and military confrontations is not an irrational departure from economic logic, but the manifestation of a structural transformation of the world economy. We develop a model of debt imperialism in which the centre sustains its dominance by issuing internationally demanded liabilities that enable persistent external deficits and reinforce dependence on the dollar and on the centre's market, while simultaneously favouring the industrial expansion of semi-peripheral economies. As these economies grow, they become potential challengers whose trajectories must be actively managed and periodically disciplined in order to preserve the hierarchy of the system. The paper confronts this framework with a wide set of international data (World Bank, IMF, UNCTAD, US Treasury and BEA). We analyse global balance-of-payments indicators from 1975 to 2023 and then examine the evolution of the United States' trade creditors and the geography and composition of foreign holdings of its external liabilities. The results identify two distinct phases: a pre-2008 hegemonic phase characterised by relatively smooth surplus recycling into the centre, and a post-2008 phase marked by growing volatility, the fragmentation of the integrated world market, the reconfiguration of trade and financial circuits, and the decline of the previous globalisation regime. This analysis shows that the fragmentation of the global economy after 2008 has not resulted from a collapse of U.S. centrality, but from a defensive reorganisation of trade, financial and geopolitical relations aimed at disciplining both allies and semi-peripheral challengers.

title: When Crime Kills Jobs: Murder and Labor-Capital Substitution in U.S. firms
affiliations: King’s College London - King's Business School

detail.title: When Crime Kills Jobs: Murder and Labor-Capital Substitution in U.S. firms
detail.abstract: We study how violent crime shapes production arrangements by examining the effects of murder shocks on labor-capital substitution in U.S. firms. Using long-run state-level murder data, policy-induced crime shocks from Stand Your Ground laws, and crimeaugmenting cocaine price shocks, we show that higher crime is associated with increases in capital-labor ratios. This adjustment is driven predominantly by employment shedding rather than by capital deepening. The effects are stronger in firms with higher operating leverage and employment rigidity and are amplified by financing frictions. Our findings uncover labor risk and financing capacity as key channels linking crime to firms' production decisions.

title: Social and Health Outcomes around Divorce: Evidence from New Zealand
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, University of Texas at Austin - College of Liberal Arts, Auckland University of Technology, Naval Postgraduate School and Auckland University of Technology - NZ Work Research Institute

detail.title: Social and Health Outcomes around Divorce: Evidence from New Zealand
detail.abstract: How does marital separation and divorce affect spouses and their children? We provide new evidence using a matched difference-indifferences design in rich administrative data from New Zealand. While most outcomes remain stable prior to separation, parents' mental health deteriorates in the lead-up. At separation, men's employment falls while women's rises, and women become much more likely to receive government benefits. Men temporarily double their police incidents; about a third of the increase is domestic violence complaints. Both parents become more likely to be the victim of non-domestic crime as well. As for mental health, parents become more anxious and depressed at separation, and these remain elevated well after the couple has parted. Their children, too, see increased risks after separation: anxiety, depression, school absenteeism, and crime victimization all rise.

title: The Role of Technological Platforms in Stimulating Innovation
affiliations: MGIMO (Moscow State University of International Relations)

detail.title: The Role of Technological Platforms in Stimulating Innovation
detail.abstract: Technological platforms, functioning as integrated digital ecosystems, play an increasingly crucial role in stimulating innovation within the modern economy. This paper examines their transformative impact on business models and the innovation process. The analysis highlights that digital ecosystems, characterized by a customer-centric architecture that consolidates diverse products, services, and data flows, significantly accelerate the diffusion of innovations by facilitating seamless interaction among users and providers. A key driver of this transformation is "uberisation," which exemplifies the restructuring of economic relationships around flexible, platform-based networks. The study specifically explores the development trajectory of such ecosystems in Russia, identifying core trends: the migration of high-tech companies to online platform solutions, the pursuit of maximum user convenience through unified applications, the application of big data analytics for personalisation, and the expansion of market access for small and medium-sized enterprises. The Russian landscape is shaped by leading players from the IT sector (e.g., Yandex, VK), telecommunications (e.g., MTS), and notably, the financial industry (e.g., Sberbank, T-Bank), where established banks leverage their extensive client bases and data resources to build comprehensive service platforms. The author concludes that digital ecosystems are not merely technological tools but fundamental strategic models that enhance competitive advantage through data-driven insights and network effects. Their proliferation fosters an innovative environment, supports entrepreneurship, and reshapes the operational paradigms of both traditional and emerging businesses.

title: The Dynamics of Volume and Open Interest in Exchange-Listed Derivatives Markets
affiliations: Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge - Department of Finance

detail.title: The Dynamics of Volume and Open Interest in Exchange-Listed Derivatives Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This paper identifies previously unrecognized structural relationships that exist in trading activity measures of the derivatives markets. The precise mathematical relationship between volume, open interest, and market entry and exit is derived as a difference equation that could be useful in future empirical research. Entry and exit are reflected in the expansion and contraction of existing positions and the creation of new positions. The results are exact and do not rely on statistical estimation or assumptions and apply broadly to all exchange-listed derivatives markets.

title: The Dual Face of Workplace AI: A Typology of Digital Work Configurations and Job Quality Implications in Europe
affiliations: University of Warwick

detail.title: The Dual Face of Workplace AI: A Typology of Digital Work Configurations and Job Quality Implications in Europe
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping European labour markets, yet research examines worker AI adoption and employer algorithmic management as separate phenomena. This paper develops a typology classifying workers into four digital work configurations based on AI tool usage intensity and algorithmic control exposure: Non-Digital Baseline, Heavily Controlled, Digitally Empowered, and Managed Augmenter. Analysing 50,462 workers across 27 EU countries from the AIM-WORK survey, the study finds substantial cross-national variation in configuration distributions and systematically different job quality outcomes across configurations. Digitally Empowered workers earn 21 percentage points more relative to country medians with preserved autonomy, whilst Heavily Controlled workers experience reduced autonomy and work intensification without compensating wage premiums. Managed Augmenters face sustained autonomy constraints despite AI access. The findings demonstrate that organisational configurations of AI and algorithmic management, not technology adoption alone, determine job quality outcomes, with implications for AI governance policies seeking to distribute benefits whilst mitigating worker harms.

title: Specifics of Risk Assessment for Transnational Business in Today’s Environment
affiliations: MGIMO (Moscow State University of International Relations)

detail.title: Specifics of Risk Assessment for Transnational Business in Today’s Environment
detail.abstract: The intensification of global economic integration, while expanding opportunities for investment and business diversification, simultaneously generates a complex array of transnational risks that demand specialized management approaches. This paper examines the specificities of risk assessment for international business operations in the contemporary environment, focusing on country risks as a fundamental category. These risks originate from systemic disparities in national legal and financial frameworks, administrative and customs barriers, varying tax regimes, and inconsistencies in the availability and reliability of information across jurisdictions. The unique institutional configuration of each sovereign state creates an environment where domestic economic, political, or legal shifts directly impact foreign commercial entities. The analysis highlights that effective risk management for transnational business is contingent upon the timely identification of emerging threats and the implementation of proactive mitigation strategies to minimise potential financial losses. In the context of evolving global trade patterns, particular attention is given to Russia's shifting foreign economic partnerships, with countries such as China, India, Turkey, Brazil, and the UAE emerging as key counterparts. This reorientation necessitates a thorough and updated assessment of the associated country risks for Russian businesses operating abroad, requiring a nuanced understanding of the specific regulatory, economic, and institutional landscapes in these regions. The study underscores that robust risk assessment is not merely a defensive measure but a critical strategic tool for ensuring the sustainability and competitiveness of international business in an interconnected yet heterogeneous global economy.

title: Managers and the Cultural Transmission of Gender Norms
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Melbourne, University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and

detail.title: Managers and the Cultural Transmission of Gender Norms

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This paper studies how managers’ gender attitudes shape workplace culture and gender inequality. Using data from a multinational firm operating in over 100 countries, we leverage cross-country manager rotations to identify the effects of male managers' gender attitudes on gender pay gaps within a team. Managers from countries with one standard deviation more progressive gender attitudes reduce the pay gap by 5 percentage points (18%), largely through higher promotion rates for women. These effects persist after managers rotate out and are strongest in more conservative countries. Managers with progressive attitudes also influence the local office culture, as local managers who interact with but are not under the purview of the foreign manager begin to have smaller pay gaps in their teams. Our evidence points to individual managers as critical in shaping corporate culture.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Well-being Increases in Age Among Workers:  Evidence From 103 Countries
affiliations: Dartmouth College - Department of Economics and University College London

detail.title: Well-being Increases in Age Among Workers:  Evidence From 103 Countries

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We examine how workers’ and non-workers’ wellbeing varies by age across 171 countries in eight international surveys. In 103 countries (60%) we find evidence that workers’ wellbeing rises with age and workers' illbeing falls with age. This relationship appears to have strengthened over time in some countries. Patterns are different among non-workers and are sensitive to survey mode. Where surveys are conducted using Computer-Assisted Web-based Interviews (CAWI) non-workers’ wellbeing is U-shaped, but this is less clear-cut when the data are collected with Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviews (CATI). The change in the age profile of workers’ wellbeing may reflect changes in selection into (out of) employment by age, changes in job quality, or changes in young workers’ orientation to similar jobs over time. But changes in smartphone usage – often the focus of debate regarding declining young peoples’ wellbeing – are unlikely to be the main culprit unless there are sizeable differences in smartphone usage across young workers and non-workers, which appears unlikely.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Trade and US Inequality in the Tokyo Round
affiliations: North Carolina State University,  and College of William and Mary - Department of Economics

detail.title: Trade and US Inequality in the Tokyo Round

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Against a backdrop of sharply rising inequality, the Tokyo Round of the GATT resulted in a 1.6 percentage point reduction in average US tariffs – larger than CUSFTA, NAFTA, and the liberalization accompanying the granting of PNTR to China. We construct a novel IV based on the so-called “Swiss formula” that governed the Tokyo Round tariff liberalization to provide evidence of its effects on imports and inequality. Instrumented tariff reductions explain approximately 20% of the rise in income inequality between non-production and production workers between 1979 and 1988. This effect is largest among women, workers in routine occupations, and workers in more technology-intensive industries, suggesting a complementarity between trade liberalization and skill-biased technological change.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: AI and Financial Stability

detail.title: AI and Financial Stability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am the sole author of this paper. I have no personal or financial relationship with other people or organizations that may have or could be perceived to have influenced their study.
declarations.funderStatement: I have received no funding for this research.

detail.abstract: Artificial-intelligence (AI) tool-kits drive credit scoring engines, shape real-time market-making algorithms and populate regulator dashboards. Because these models co-evolve with the financial system they steer, the old "exogenous-shock" lens used to analyze and discuss financial stability is no longer sufficient. Moreover, the centrality of time-varying non-linearities and feedback effects for measuring systemic risk cannot be ignored, as has often been the case in the post-global financial crisis' empirical literature. This paper makes two assumptions: first, that the objective of financial stability is to minimize systemic risk, which is viewed as endogenous to the macrofinancial system. Second, systemic risk can take three forms, as a global shock to the financial system, as contagion among financial institutions and as slow buildup of vulnerabilities, all of which end up eventually negatively affecting the real economy (ECB, 2009). The paper explores how and through which channels AI may reshape systemic risk, and tests whether the extensive application of AI in the EU banking industry in the last decade has had any significant effect on systemic risk as predicted in the literature. The paper makes three contributions. First, it synthesizes the fragmented conceptual and policy literature into a single internally coherent framework mapped onto the three forms of systemic risk. Second, it analyzes the most recent empirical studies that test whether hypotheses are verified or falsified. Thirdly, it uses a statistical model that has proven useful to measure the three forms that systemic risk can take to test several theoretical predictions regarding the impact of AI on financial stability. The main findings include; (1) evidence of an increase in the volatility of short-term measures of contagion; (2) indication of an increase systemic risk in the form of a global shock and heightened interdependence among banks; (3) no evidence of a rise in banks' asset price correlation; (4) clouding of the distinction between global and idiosyncratic shocks; (5) no increase in the procyclicality of systemic risk as a result of the diffusion of AI in the banking sector in the euro area. These findings suggest that regulators and supervisors need to adapt to the rapidly changing banking industry's environment as a result of AI diffusion.

title: Banking on Inattention
affiliations: University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business and NYU Stern School of Business

detail.title: Banking on Inattention

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We demonstrate that depositor inattention gives rise to banks’ deposit market power. Using transaction-level data on millions of U.S. depositors, we document that unscheduled income remains in low-rate accounts much longer than scheduled income, and interpret this reaction-time gap as inattention. Inattention varies widely across depositors, and more inattentive depositors adjust their balances less in response to monetary policy changes. We then develop and test a theory of temporal monopoly to analyze the implications of inattention for bank funding. Banks face an intertemporal trade-off in deposit rate setting between current spreads and the future deposit base, modulated by inattention. In line with this theory, we find that banks serving more inattentive depositors set lower rates, have weaker pass-through, and experience less deposit flow sensitivity. Using these estimates, we calibrate how the value of banks’ deposit franchise rises with inattention and varies nonmonotonically with the policy rate. Our results shed new light on how digital banking and monetary policy affect deposit funding.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Ensuring of National Technological Sovereignty
affiliations: MGIMO (Moscow State University of International Relations)

detail.title: Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Ensuring of National Technological Sovereignty
detail.abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has become a central element of global strategic competition and a key factor in ensuring national technological sovereignty. This paper examines the dual nature of international innovation activity: while it facilitates the cross-border transfer of knowledge and stimulates structural economic changes, it simultaneously poses significant challenges to domestic competitive landscapes and state sovereignty through the activities of high-tech transnational corporations. The evolving "cold technology war," particularly between major powers, underscores the growing politicization of science and technology, potentially leading to a fragmentation of global innovation networks and a strategic retreat of R&D activities within national borders. Against this backdrop of escalating geopolitical tensions and restricted access to foreign technologies, the imperative for Russia to achieve technological sovereignty, especially in the field of AI, is critically analyzed. The study identifies persisting structural dependencies in Russia's foreign trade, notably in high-tech imports, while highlighting a decisive reorientation of economic partnerships towards nations such as China, India, Turkey, Brazil, and the UAE. This shift presents both challenges and new avenues for international cooperation in innovation. The author argues that achieving technological sovereignty and sustainable AI development requires a synergistic and adaptive national strategy. This strategy must integrate effective state programmes, foster close collaboration between academia, industry, and the state, and attract private investment through targeted support measures. The implementation of targeted national projects and strategic public-private partnerships with leading domestic corporations (e.g., Rostec, Rostelecom, Sberbank) in priority technological domains is identified as a crucial mechanism. The paper concludes that, leveraging its historical scientific and engineering strengths, Russia possesses the foundational capacity to navigate contemporary geopolitical instability, transform it into a catalyst for developing indigenous technologies with unique characteristics, and thereby secure its position in the emerging global technological order.

title: Housing Market Responses to Mandatory Flood Risk Disclosure
affiliations: and University of Antwerp

detail.title: Housing Market Responses to Mandatory Flood Risk Disclosure
detail.abstract: We study the causal effects of flood risk disclosure in housing markets. We exploit a 2013 reform mandating flood risk disclosure in real estate listings in Flanders (Belgium), combined with the universe of real estate transactions and difference-in-differences and difference-in-discontinuity designs. We find that disclosure reduced house prices in medium-risk flood zones by about 4 percent. In high-risk zones, price effects arise only at flood-risk boundaries, consistent with disclosure increasing the salience of flood risk exposure. In medium-risk areas, price declines are larger in lower–socioeconomic-status neighborhoods, and buyers are less likely to come from lower socioeconomic neighborhoods after disclosure. These results indicate that information frictions were more pronounced among socioeconomically vulnerable households prior to disclosure.

title: Surfactants: Molecular Classification, Interfacial Behavior, Industrial Applications, and Environmental Implications

detail.abstract: Surfactants are amphiphilic compounds that play a foundational role in modern chemical, biological, and industrial systems by modulating interfacial phenomena. Their ability to self-assemble into micelles, reduce surface and interfacial tension, and solubilize otherwise immiscible phases has enabled widespread application across detergents, pharmaceuticals, agriculture, environmental remediation, and pulmonary medicine. This paper provides a comprehensive review of surfactants from a molecular, functional, and application-driven perspective. Key classification systems including ionic, nonionic, zwitterionic structures and hydrophile lipophile balance (HLB) are critically examined alongside physicochemical properties such as critical micelle concentration, cloud point, and Krafft point. The review integrates industrial-scale usage patterns, environmental transport and ecotoxicity, biomedical roles of pulmonary surfactants, and emerging technologies such as biosensors and ionic liquid-based surfactants.

title: Structural Negotiability: From Primeval Rights to Land to Neoprimeval Rights to System Rents
affiliations: Clean Technology Hub

detail.title: Structural Negotiability: From Primeval Rights to Land to Neoprimeval Rights to System Rents
detail.abstract: Prevailing economic theory justifies inequality as the efficient outcome of marginal productivity, rewarding capital and labour for their respective contributions. This paper challenges that foundation by developing the theory of structural negotiability. It posits that a primeval right to an equal share of land for all humans in a given society exists, but due to injustice, limits of taxation, and tolerability of “sub-primeval” justice, was systematically flouted. While the transition to capitalism further undermined primeval rights—which Henry George would challenge at the end of the 19th century—, industrial capitalism created system rents that act as “natural” resources, necessitating the invocation of a “neoprimeval right”. Distributive justice in modern economies therefore requires the conscious negotiation of three concurrent imperatives: (1) the neoprimeval right to a share of socially-created "system rents" embedded in Total Factor Productivity (TFP)—such as gains from agglomeration, innovation, public institutions, and network effects, (2) the efficiency imperative of functional property rights that reward marginal productivity, and (3) the fence right to institutions that ensure balanced bargaining power The analysis demonstrates that the standard model, which sanctifies the residual claim of capital while compensating labor solely for its marginal product, operates as an engine for systemic inequity, systematically directing the vast majority of TFP growth toward capital holders. Ultimately, honouring the collective claim to social wealth requires moving beyond redistributive taxation to pre-distributive institutional design: a more egalitarian distribution of system rents, broadening capital ownership via sovereign wealth funds and employee trusts, and fortifying new forms of collective bargaining.

title: Changing Culture and Norms in Developing Countries
affiliations: Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) and University of Zurich

detail.title: Changing Culture and Norms in Developing Countries

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We survey recent research on changing culture and social norms in developing countries and propose a simple framework to interpret these changes. We conceptualize individual utility from a given action as a function of three components: intrinsic valuations, material payoffs, and social interactions. Using this lens, we review evidence on interventions that target each component and their interactions.First, we discuss efforts to shift intrinsic values through schooling and curricula, information campaigns, mass media, and empowerment programs, with particular attention to gender norms, intimate partner violence, and harmful practices such as female genital cutting. Second, we examine social determinants of behavior, including misperceptions about others’ beliefs, coordination failures, and the role of intermediate “stepping-stone” actions in facilitating or hindering norm transitions. Third, we analyze how changes in material incentives, via labor market opportunities, transfers, and legal reforms, affect behavior and underlying norms.Throughout, we highlight methodological challenges in measuring norms and identifying mechanisms, and we emphasize that policy effects depend critically on existing social structures and belief distributions. We conclude by outlining open questions from a positive and normative perspective.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

detail.abstract: The Russian Civil Code, in its Part Four, provides for a large number of situations in which copyright protection is granted unilaterally. title: Sovereign ESG and the Social Guarantee: Universal Basic Income as a Catalyst for National Stability, Capacity Building, and Sufficient Sustainable  Trust to End Poverty
affiliations: Swiss School Of Business and Management

detail.title: Sovereign ESG and the Social Guarantee: Universal Basic Income as a Catalyst for National Stability, Capacity Building, and Sufficient Sustainable  Trust to End Poverty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: n/a
declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract:
The global landscape of the mid-2020s is defined by a "poly-crisis": the simultaneous convergence of accelerating climate degradation, widening economic inequality, and a precipitous decline in trust toward national institutions. For sovereign leaders and policymakers, these are not merely social challenges but material risks that directly impact national creditworthiness, cost of capital, and long-term stability. The traditional social contract, predicated on 20th-century labor market dynamics and conditional welfare models, is increasingly viewed by sovereign risk analysts as insufficient for the volatility of the modern era. 
This Applied Research Report provides an exhaustive analysis of Universal Basic Income (UBI) not as a utopian ideal, but as a pragmatic macro-structural instrument to enhance Sovereign Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) performance. By decoupling from labor market volatility, UBI builds national capacity in self-sufficiency and sustainability skills, thereby stabilizing the "Social" (S) pillar of sovereign credit ratings and restoring the "Governance" (G) pillar through enhanced public trust.The analysis synthesizes data from over 200 distinct research sources, covering major pilots in Kenya, Finland, Stockton (USA), and India, as well as sovereign debt reports from the World Bank, IMF, and major credit rating agencies. The evidence suggests that unconditional cash transfers function as "liquidity for agency," enabling populations to invest in vocational training, transition to green energy sources, and engage in risk-taking entrepreneurship. Furthermore, when funded through sovereign wealth mechanisms or carbon pricing, UBI provides a fiscal logic for the green transition, transforming the proceeds of environmental regulation into tangible social dividends.

title: "The Problem of Providing High-Tech Production Personnel in EAEU Countries: Current Status, Challenges, and Prospects" Presentation at the 5th Scientific and Practical Conference with International Participation "Human Potential — a Resource and Factor for Russia's Development"
affiliations: Moscow State Institute for International Relations (MGIMO-University)

detail.title: "The Problem of Providing High-Tech Production Personnel in EAEU Countries: Current Status, Challenges, and Prospects" Presentation at the 5th Scientific and Practical Conference with International Participation "Human Potential — a Resource and Factor for Russia's Development"
detail.abstract: Currently, the strategic development priority of the EAEU member countries is economic modernization, which aims to transition to a new technological paradigm based on the use of artificial intelligence, industrial robotics, and big data analysis. Achieving this ambitious goal is impossible without changes in the employment structure, improved worker skills, and improved human capital. This report, based on statistical data, examines the growth dynamics of high-tech manufacturing in EAEU member countries, analyzes changes in the labor market, identifies the most in-demand specialties, and examines advances in the training of specialists in engineering and scientific fields. The author concludes that the efforts of the government, the professional community, and the higher education systems of EAEU countries to provide high-tech manufacturing with personnel trained by their universities are insufficient. The author identifies the causes and potential consequences, identifies prospects, and makes recommendations for improving the training of specialists for high-tech manufacturing.

title: Proportional Recovery And Incentives To Settle
affiliations: United States Court of Appeals, Fifth Circuit

detail.title: Proportional Recovery And Incentives To Settle

declarations.ethicsApproval: Experiment subjects consented to participate. The research was approved by the University at Buffalo's IRB.

detail.abstract:
Proportional recovery allows plaintiffs to recover damages prorated by some percentage proven at trial. The typical example of proportional recovery in modern tort law is the loss-of-chance doctrine, which allows medical malpractice plaintiffs to recover damages using probabilistic evidence of causation, with damages proportional to the probability of causation they can demonstrate. Advances in scientific data on attributable risks and causation, together with ongoing academic debates, are likely to prompt courts to consider expanding proportional recovery rules in tort law. 

This Article examines how proportional recovery rules affect parties’ incentives to settle lawsuits. It presents the results of a vignette experiment designed to test how proportional recovery rules, such as the loss-of-chance doctrine, affect litigation risk. Subjects considered several legal scenarios, were randomly assigned to evaluate them under traditional causation and recovery rules or a proportional approach, and were asked whether they would prefer to settle or litigate their claims. The experiment reveals that subjects facing proportional recovery rules were 12 percentage points more likely to settle their claims. Subjects facing proportional causation and recovery were also willing to accept settlement offers that were approximately 8% smaller. The results suggest that reductions in administrative costs are a yet-unidentified benefit to proportional causation. Moreover, they indicate that the current approach to the loss-of-chance doctrine in medical malpractice, which only permits low-probability plaintiffs to recover proportional damages, exposes courts to the downsides of proportional recovery without the corresponding administrative benefits the experiment identifies.

title: Finding Our Compass: Reflections on a World in Crisis

detail.title: Finding Our Compass: Reflections on a World in Crisis
detail.abstract:
"There's a time when the operation of the Machine becomes so odious, makes you so sick at heart, that you can't take part, you can't even passively take part." So said Mario Savio in 1964; so say millions of the disenfranchised now. As the apparatus of elite institutions grinds on, pushing society to the brink, protesters across the world are putting their bodies upon its gears and its wheels, to open up space for freedom and creativity unconstrained by institutional strictures. It's time we all followed their lead.
 
In a series of free-wheeling reflections and summaries of historical scholarship, this book reinterprets history and culture along anarchist lines. From a rationalistic and Marxian point of view it illuminates capitalism, U.S. history, popular culture, gender relations, and human psychology, even the nature of the intriguing concepts "genius" and "greatness." Its agenda is that of the seventeenth-century Levellers: deflate the pomposities of elite authority, and bring the world down to the level of democratic reason. In the process, one hopes, we will find our way out of the crisis of the present and into a more just civilization in the future.

title: Return Spillovers in Corporate Bonds
affiliations: Reichman University - Interdisciplinary Center (IDC) Herzliyah, George Washington University - Department of Finance and Donald G. Costello College of Business at George Mason University

detail.title: Return Spillovers in Corporate Bonds
detail.abstract: This paper shows that corporate bond return predictability systematically propagates across bonds. We develop a structured, self-financing optimization framework that maps lead-lag autocovariances into dynamic long-short portfolios with closed-form weights and expected profitability. The framework delivers a transparent decomposition of predictability into own-bond continuation and cross-bond transmission, isolating components incremental to standard momentum. Using ICE and TRACE data, we find that spillovers account for a substantial share of profitability, especially among higher-credit-risk portfolios. The resulting strategies exhibit strong and persistent out-of-sample performance. Cross-sectional patterns are consistent with gradual price adjustment to evolving credit-risk conditions.

title: The Accounting Blind Spot in Public Infrastructure and Public Goods

detail.title: The Accounting Blind Spot in Public Infrastructure and Public Goods

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Public infrastructure and public goods are increasingly delivered through financialised models such as public-private partnerships, despite extensive evidence of higher long-term costs, rigidity, and fiscal risk. This paper argues that the persistence of these models is driven less by their economic performance than by how public-sector accounting systems classify capital, obligations, and time. Contemporary public accounting frameworks are designed to enforce annual fiscal discipline and debt control, not to represent long-horizon capital continuity or mission-aligned renewal. 
As a result, delivery models that defer recognition of obligations, smooth expenditures across reporting periods, or shift commitments off balance sheet appear fiscally responsible even when they embed greater long-term fragility. The paper shows that public accounting does not merely record infrastructure choices but actively structures them by rendering capital continuity, mission cycles, and deferred fragility invisible. The persistence of financialised delivery models is therefore an accounting outcome rather than a policy anomaly. The paper concludes that accounting reform alone cannot resolve this blind spot; addressing it requires a conceptual expansion of public finance beyond flow-based and liability-centred representations of public capital.

detail.abstract: Despite the high value placed on social connection, recent data indicates a severe "friendship recession," particularly among men, and a startling lack of reciprocity in social ties; studies suggest only 50% of perceived friendships are reciprocal. This paper proposes that the current crisis is exacerbated by "Relational Anosognosia"—a phenomenon where individuals lack the external self-awareness to recognize their social deficits, distinct from psychological denial. By synthesizing Tasha Eurich’s research on self-awareness gaps, the clinical pathology of anosognosia, and Social Exchange Theory, this paper identifies a significant underserved opportunity: the creation of diagnostic and feedback mechanisms (akin to 360-degree reviews and LEAP protocols) designed specifically for non-clinical social impairment.

title: Credit Risk and the Private Equity J-Curve: A Framework for Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
affiliations: INSEAD and Singapore University of Social Science

detail.title: Credit Risk and the Private Equity J-Curve: A Framework for Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement
detail.abstract: Private equity performance metrics recognize credit risk only when losses materialize, ignoring embedded default risk from the moment leverage is deployed. We develop a framework integrating Expected Credit Loss (ECL) methodology with J-curve analysis to quantify this forward-looking risk dimension. The framework complements rather than replaces traditional metrics, revealing probability-weighted downside exposure that peaks during re-commitment decisions for successor funds. Illustrative calibrations suggest embedded credit risk varies meaningfully with vintage year, sector concentration, asset composition, and GP quality - though external validation requires proprietary portfolio company default data that remains unavailable. We discuss potential applications for portfolio construction and performance evaluation.
