Credit card issuers deploy sophisticated algorithms that continuously analyze consumer spending and borrowing behaviors, often increasing credit limits without consumers requesting such changes.

title: Green skepticism, competition, and welfare in vertically differentiated markets
affiliations: University of Toulon

detail.title: Green skepticism, competition, and welfare in vertically differentiated markets
detail.abstract: This paper explores the effects of green skepticism on market competition, the environment, and welfare within a vertical differentiation model. Two firms offer a green and a brown product and compete on price. Consumers differ in their beliefs about the environmental quality of the products. Some consumers trust the environmental quality, while others are skeptical. We show how green skepticism influences competition through two channels: the degree of skepticism, which alters perceived product differentiation, and its spread, which shapes market demand. We show that the effects of green skepticism are non-monotonic. Moderate and widespread skepticism collapses perceived differentiation, intensifies price competition, and results in a brown monopoly. This leads to an "environmental trap" with the worst quality of the environment. When green production costs are low, green skepticism generally shifts consumption toward brown products, thereby degrading the environment and welfare. Conversely, when green production costs are high, a limited share of highly skeptical consumers can benefit both firms while improving quality of the environment. Welfare outcomes depend on the regulator's objectives. A populist regulator focused primarily on economic welfare derived from perceived product qualities would support green skepticism. However, a paternalistic regulator concerned about environmental externalities and focused on economic welfare derived from actual product qualities would face a trade-off between economic efficiency, which requires moderate and widespread skepticism, and environmental protection, which requires full confidence. Thus, when green products entail significant production costs, combating green skepticism does not always improve welfare and enhance the environment.

title: Administrative Centralization & Urban Authoritarianism: Voting Behaviour in Maharashtra's 2026 Municipal Corporation Elections
affiliations: and Regent College London

detail.title: Administrative Centralization & Urban Authoritarianism: Voting Behaviour in Maharashtra's 2026 Municipal Corporation Elections

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known personal, professional, or financial relationships with individuals or organizations that could have influenced, or be perceived to have influenced, the research presented in this study. The analysis and conclusions are based solely on independent research, publicly available data, and academic sources.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human participants, patient data, interviews, or experimental subjects. It is based entirely on secondary data, publicly available sources, policy documents, and academic literature. As such, formal ethics committee approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: Funder Statement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from public, commercial, or non-profit funding agencies. The study was independently conducted by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper critically examines voting behaviour and electoral administration in contemporary democracies through an empirical analysis of the 15 January 2026 Maharashtra state municipal corporation elections in India. It interrogates the weight of religious majoritarianism, financial inducements, institutional capture, misinformation, and development-oriented rhetoric in shaping urban electoral outcomes. Drawing on political anthropology and behavioural economics, the study analyses how voter psychology is systematically mobilised through identity-based narratives, fear, institutional threats, manipulation of electoral instruments and accessories and short-term incentives. This paper argues that frequently displaces substantive considerations of urban governance and long-term development intentionally by ruling parties. Based on field-based observation, quantitative and qualitative evidence, the research demonstrates how political parties, in conjunction with professional consultancies and media war room influences, penetrate electoral processes and local public institutions, thereby normalising corruption-linked practices. By contrasting these electoral strategies with citizens’ articulated material priorities including water, environment, infrastructure, education, employment, business growth, smooth banking, healthcare and real estate development, the paper constructs an analytical framework mapping electoral manipulation technique against public-interest requirements. It argues that the resulting disjunction reflects a structural fascism breaking democratic choice rather than meaningful political participation. The study concludes by advancing a development centred model of electoral accountability that foregrounds institutional neutrality, administrative integrity, and governance outcomes as prerequisites for democratic legitimacy.

title: Extreme Weather, Public Concern, and Adaptation Policy: Evidence from Citizen–Government Interactions in China
affiliations: University of Cambridge - Faculty of Economics and Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Institutes of Science and Development

detail.title: Extreme Weather, Public Concern, and Adaptation Policy: Evidence from Citizen–Government Interactions in China
detail.abstract: We provide the first systematic high-frequency evidence on the intensity and dynamics of public hazard concern around extreme weather exposure. Using over 200,000 citizen messages posted to China’s Message Board for Leaders between 2011 and 2023, we construct monthly, prefecture-level measures of hazard concern and link them to exposure to temperature extremes, heavy precipitation, haze, and drought. Temperature extremes and heavy precipitation generate pronounced but short-lived spikes in hazard concern, with effects fading within one to two months. This indicates a narrow window for targeted communication to most effectively support attribution and belief updating. Notably, concern responses are heterogeneous across regions, are amplified in cities with more active government engagement in communication with citizens, and exhibit spillovers to indirectly exposed locations following particularly severe, nationally salient extreme events. We further show that heightened concern expression predicts increases in local policy attention in subsequent government work reports for hydrological hazards, but not for temperature extremes or haze.

title: No Refund, No Problem: Coordination and Cooperation in a Combined Linear-Threshold Public Good Game
affiliations: Williams College and University of Massachusetts Amherst

detail.title: No Refund, No Problem: Coordination and Cooperation in a Combined Linear-Threshold Public Good Game
detail.abstract: We use a lab experiment to study a combined linear-threshold public good game, with linear returns to contributions and an additional higher return if a threshold is met. This game structure leverages both voluntary cooperation and strategic coordination. We experimentally vary what happens to contributions that do not meet the threshold. Contributions are high, with almost all groups reaching the threshold. Refund institutions matter, but only a little: contributions are only slightly higher on average if insufficient contributions are automatically refunded than if they are not refunded. However, optional refunds chosen ex post perform relatively poorly. Risk aversion causes people to reduce their contributions when insufficient contributions are automatically refunded, so that treatment differences are even smaller for risk averse people. An online survey-experiment shows that people perceive refunds in this institution as desirable from a donor’s perspective. However, a donor’s taking advantage of a refund is perceived as non-normative, and this becomes even more true in a naturalistic charity context, pointing to the importance of domain-specific norms in situations like this with complex incentives and social dynamics.

title: Strategic Residual Emissions in Net Emissions Targets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Strategic Residual Emissions in Net Emissions Targets
detail.abstract: Net emissions targets require balancing out remaining residual emissions with carbon removals. While an increasing number of countries are adopting such targets, it remains unclear how governments determine the level of residual emissions at which they plan to achieve them. This paper examines the role of strategic environmental policy in shaping this choice. Using a theoretical model of two regions trading a polluting good and carbon removals, I show that governments have strategic incentives to unilaterally deviate from first-best residual emissions to enhance domestic welfare. Under imperfect competition, the optimal unilateral policy leads to inefficiently high residual emissions, partly due to rent-shifting motives that could be referred to as removal dumping. A numerical illustration suggests that these effects can be quantitatively significant: unilaterally optimal residual emissions in the German steel sector are nearly twice as high as the cooperative level, increasing German industry profits by about one percent. However, the sign and magnitude of the distortion generally depend on the assumed market structure. Finally, I discuss how unilateral strategic incentives are influenced by the type of net emissions target adopted in other regions.

title: Effects of Environmental Subsidy and Consumer Eco-consciousness on Firm's Green Replacement Under Asymmetric Competition
affiliations: Chongqing University, Tianjin University, Chongqing University and Loughborough University

detail.title: Effects of Environmental Subsidy and Consumer Eco-consciousness on Firm's Green Replacement Under Asymmetric Competition
detail.abstract: Amid urgent decarbonization needs and the constraints of green innovation costs and risks, firms across industries are adopting green replacement by partially substituting emission-intensive methods with greener alternatives to produce quasi-green products (QGPs). Central to this strategy is the green-replacing ratio decision, which determines the QGP's cost structure, emission profile, and potential price premium, while also incurring incremental costs for the firms. This study employs a game-theoretic model to analyze how consumer eco-consciousness and an environmental subsidy proportional to the green-replacing ratio influence a firm's green replacement under asymmetric competition with a traditional rival. We find that the green-replacing ratio depends on the GF's strategic trade-off among the product-differentiating effect, the profit-margin effect, and the intention to avoid the free-riding threat. The unit subsidy can diminish or eliminate the free-riding threat, thus improving the green-replacing ratio. We also uncover an excessive-premium distortion, where a lower green-replacing ratio paradoxically commands a higher QGP premium, hurting the consumers. Interestingly, either the free-riding threat or a specifically calibrated unit subsidy can eliminate this distortion under certain conditions. Moreover, while a unit subsidy reduces both emissions intensity and total emissions under low-to-moderate eco-consciousness, it increases total emissions without affecting emissions intensity under high eco-consciousness.

title: Does Paying for Data Change Investment Decisions?
affiliations: University of Duisburg-Essen - Institute of Political Science, , University of Toronto - Finance Area and University of Calgary - Haskayne School of Business

detail.title: Does Paying for Data Change Investment Decisions?

declarations.ethicsApproval: We obtained ethics approval from the University of Calgary Research Board (certificate: REB25-1876)
declarations.funderStatement: Marius Zoican acknowledges funding from the Canada Research Chairs Program and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC Insight Grant 435-2025-0100). Mariana Khapko acknowledges funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC Insight Grant 435-2025-0882).

detail.abstract: Do investors trade differently when paying for market data versus getting it for free? In an investment experiment, we randomize whether subjects pay for or freely receive identical order flow data. Payment inflates perceived data informativeness by 11%, increases responsiveness of return forecasts to data by 31%, and leads to 14% larger forecast errors. We further document a sunk-cost mechanism concentrated among low financial literacy investors: payment raises investment levels while reducing the response of investment to own return forecasts. Offering data as a paid add-on distorts beliefs and behavior, with the burden falling disproportionately on the least sophisticated investors.

title: U.S. Tariff Announcements and Financial Markets: Evidence from the S&P 500, VIX, and CPI

detail.title: U.S. Tariff Announcements and Financial Markets: Evidence from the S&P 500, VIX, and CPI
detail.abstract:
This study examines the impact of US tariffs, Market Volatility (VIX), and Inflation (CPI) on the financial market. The study focuses on three key indicators these includes; S&P 500 index, the VIX index, and the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Tariff announcements increase or decrease the cost for businesses and consumers. Tariffs also create uncertainty in the financial market.

It was found that tariff brings significant increase in the S&P 500. The stock prices became unstable when the tariff was announced. It was also found that daily return shows higher fluctuation when tariffs are announced. This has shown that the investors react instantly to trade policy news. Market volatility increases when there is uncertainty about the tariff. VIX index increases after big tariff announcements and indicates increased investor fear and doubt. When tariffs are lowered or suspended, volatility is eliminated, and markets become stable.

In 2026 the study predicts a slight rise in the S&P500. It is anticipated that the VIX is expected to remain in the range of 15 to 20 only with brief bursts in case of a shock. Unless tariffs increase the price of imports dramatically, the CPI ought to move somewhat downward. All in all, the research arrives at a conclusion that tariffs primarily introduce short run volatility and noise into the financial markets. Little impact on the basic drivers of the economy occurs unless used in conjunction with large and protracted shocks.

title: Age Verification Laws and Population Mental Health
affiliations: Capital University of Economics and Business and University of West Georgia

detail.title: Age Verification Laws and Population Mental Health
detail.abstract: This study provides the first estimates of the mental health effects of state age verification laws (AVLs), which require pornographic websites to verify that users are over 18. In response, the largest adult-content platform exited nearly all AVL states. Using Google Trends data, we document disruptions to habitual browsing: AVLs are associated with sharp declines in search interest for the dominant compliant platform, accompanied by substantial substitution towards noncompliant sites and increased searches for circumvention tools. We then leverage individual-level data from the Household Pulse Survey and find robust evidence that AVLs increase self-reported anxiety symptoms among adult men, with stronger impacts for younger, single, and non-white individuals. Event-study estimates indicate that these effects are short-lived, consistent with psychological frictions from disrupted status quo. In contrast, we find minimal mental health effects among women. Our findings suggest that online content regulation aimed at protecting children may have unintended consequences for the broader population.

reference: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 963
title: Corporate Mobility and Macroeconomic Statistics: Evidence from the Redomiciliations of Italian Companies
affiliations: Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy, Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Corporate Mobility and Macroeconomic Statistics: Evidence from the Redomiciliations of Italian Companies

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 963
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper examines the instances of redomiciliation by Italian multinational enterprises (MNEs) between 2012 and 2024, focusing on their reasons, their macroeconomic impacts, and on the statistical challenges involved in the analysis. Over the period in question, sixteen Italian firms, with a total market capitalization of €280 billion, relocated their legal headquarters abroad. The largest share of firms moved to the Netherlands, largely motivated by the country’s governance framework, which allows for multiple voting structures that strengthen the position of controlling shareholders. In most of the remaining cases, the redomiciliation followed the merger with a foreign competitor or a process of corporate restructuring. These redomiciliations significantly impacted Italy’s macroeconomic statistics, particularly as regards its international portfolio and direct investment position, and slightly reduced gross national income (GNI). In the study, we highlight a number of conceptual and practical challenges for statisticians, including residency classification and data compilation, and underscore the need for international standards to address these issues. Monitoring and transparent reporting are crucial for countries affected by (such) corporate mobility.

reference: New Zealand Journal of Research on Europe (2025), 19(1), 35-43
title: Why New Zealand needs European investment: Towards New Zealand-European endeavours
affiliations: University of Auckland Business School

detail.title: Why New Zealand needs European investment: Towards New Zealand-European endeavours

publicationDetails.detailsText: New Zealand Journal of Research on Europe (2025), 19(1), 35-43

detail.abstract: This editorial explores why New Zealand needs European investment. It offers several connected arguments. First, as investment is an important driver of future prosperity, New Zealand needs to stay in an open dialogue with foreign investors (including Europeans) who can aid in meeting our national and international goals (such as mitigating/adapting to the climate crisis). Second, the EU is already contributing to New Zealand’s investment needs (being the 5th largest foreign investor) but given EU’s size and our value alignment in a geopolitically fracturing world, EU’s role can be increased and its investment more actively sought via regulatory change, such as the reform of New Zealand’s Overseas Investment Act. Third, New Zealand is not here only as a “target market” for EU investment or to trade with the EU. It can also offer European partners pockets of expertise in niche areas such as space economy and bioeconomy, and contribute both knowledge and investment towards mutually beneficial and innovative “New Zealand - European endeavours.” While acknowledging the histories that shape us, Aotearoa New Zealand can pursue a forward-looking partnership with Europe – one that emphasises shared endeavours, mutual investment, and co-created futures.

title: Wav2Arrest 2.0: Long-Horizon Cardiac Arrest Prediction with Time-to-Event Modeling, Identity-Invariance, and Pseudo-Lab Alignment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Nihon Kohden Digital Health Solutions, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Emory University

detail.title: Wav2Arrest 2.0: Long-Horizon Cardiac Arrest Prediction with Time-to-Event Modeling, Identity-Invariance, and Pseudo-Lab Alignment
detail.abstract: High-frequency physiological waveform modality offers deep, real-time insights into patient status. Recently, physiological foundation models based on Photoplethysmography (PPG), such as PPG-GPT, have been shown to predict critical events, including Cardiac Arrest (CA). However, their powerful representation still needs to be leveraged suitably, especially when the downstream data/label is scarce. We offer three orthogonal improvements to improve PPG-only CA systems by using minimal auxiliary information. First, we propose to use time-to-event modeling, either through simple regression to the event onset time or by pursuing fine-grained discrete survival modeling. Second, we encourage the model to learn CA-focused features by making them patient-identity invariant. This is achieved by first training the largest-scale de-identified biometric identification model, referred to as the p-vector, and subsequently using it adversarially to deconfound cues, such as person identity, that may cause overfitting through memorization. Third, we propose regression on the pseudo-lab values generated by pre-trained auxiliary estimator networks. This is crucial since true blood lab measurements, such as lactate, sodium, troponin, and potassium, are collected sparingly. Via zero-shot prediction, the auxiliary networks can enrich cardiac arrest waveform labels and generate pseudo-continuous estimates as targets. Our proposals can independently improve the 24-hour time-averaged AUC from the 0.74 to the 0.78-0.80 range. We primarily improve over longer time horizons with minimal degradation near the event, thus pushing the Early Warning System research. Finally, we pursue multi-task formulation and diagnose it with a high gradient conflict rate among competing losses, which we alleviate via the PCGrad optimization technique.

reference: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 965
title: An Examination of the Domestic Macroeconomic Consequences of the United States’ Trade Policies
affiliations: Bank of Italy and European Central Bank (ECB)

detail.title: An Examination of the Domestic Macroeconomic Consequences of the United States’ Trade Policies

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 965
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper analyses the domestic effects of U.S. trade policies, focusing on the 2018-19 trade war and the escalation of trade tensions in 2025. In 2018-19, the U.S. imposed tariffs on just short of 18 per cent of imports, mainly from China, raising the effective tariff rate vis-à-vis the latter from 3 to 11 per cent. These tariffs mostly raised costs for U.S. consumers and firms, with near-complete pass-through to import prices, higher consumer prices, supply-chain disruptions, and job losses. Trade diversion reduced reliance on China but left the overall U.S. trade deficit broadly unchanged, while subsidies to farmers offset part of the fiscal revenues. General equilibrium estimates point to modest but non-negligible output and welfare losses. The 2025 trade war represents a qualitatively different shock: tariffs now cover most products and countries, with effective rates at 19 per cent overall and above 40 per cent for China (the latter potentially exceeding 100 per cent if truces are not renewed), and could cause input costs to rise sharply across industries. Preliminary evidence suggests partial tariff absorption by exporters, and also a substantial pass-through to U.S. consumer prices. The dollar’s unexpected depreciation is in contrast with historical patterns and could set in motion more pronounced trade balance effects; fiscal revenues will be much larger. Looking ahead, uncertainty remains high. A failure to extend truces and to deliver on the trade deals could lead to shortages of critical inputs and reinforce inflationary pressures; also, it would reignite the risk of retaliation – which has been limited, so far – potentially triggering a global demand shock.

reference: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 964
title: The Bank-Based Transmission of the 2024-25 Monetary Policy Easing in the Euro Area
affiliations: Banca d’Italia and Bank of Italy

detail.title: The Bank-Based Transmission of the 2024-25 Monetary Policy Easing in the Euro Area

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Occasional Paper No. 964
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: This paper assesses the intensity with which the monetary policy easing that began in June 2024 was transmitted to banks’ funding costs and lending rates in the euro area up to May 2025. Compared with the 2008-09 easing cycle, the pass-through to banks’ funding costs was somewhat weaker, mainly due to a dampened transmission to overnight deposit rates. Conversely, the pass-through to lending rates for firms was slightly stronger, reflecting banks’ relatively muted risk perception compared with the 2008-09 easing cycle. An analysis based on a Vector Error Correction Model on a broader sample shows that large variations in risk perception may drive a wedge between reference rates and bank lending rates. However, in the easing cycle that started in June 2024 the dynamics of banks’ risk perception were relatively subdued and, as a consequence, the transmission of reference rates to lending rates was strong.

reference: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1493
title: Global Risk Aversion and the Term Premium Gap in Emerging Market Economies
affiliations: Bank of Italy and Bank of Italy

detail.title: Global Risk Aversion and the Term Premium Gap in Emerging Market Economies

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1493
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: In this paper we analyze the impact of shocks to global risk aversion on the term structure of sovereign spreads between emerging market economies (EMEs) and the US economy. Focusing on the difference between long- and short-term spreads (i.e. the term premium gap), we find that an increase in global risk aversion reduces the term premium gap. This finding is consistent with the evidence that, during crises, EMEs experience a higher risk of default with respect to safe advanced economies, and to a greater extent at shorter maturities.

title: Behavioural and Economic Drivers of Household Preferences for Energy Retrofit Programmes: Evidence from a Discrete Choice Experiment in the Netherlands
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, VU University Amsterdam - Institute for Environmental Studies (IVM), King's College London, Technische Hochschule Ingolstadt and University College Dublin

detail.title: Behavioural and Economic Drivers of Household Preferences for Energy Retrofit Programmes: Evidence from a Discrete Choice Experiment in the Netherlands
detail.abstract: Household retrofit decisions are shaped by economic constraints and behavioural frictions. Using a pre-registered discrete choice experiment with a nationally representative sample of 2,200 Dutch households, we (1) estimate willingness to pay for six key attributes of energy retrofit programmes—upfront cost, municipal energy advisory services, CO2 savings, payback time, comfort and disruptiveness—and (2) examine how four behavioural mechanisms—risk aversion, loss aversion, status quo bias and present bias—shape preferences over these attributes. We find that Dutch households are willing to pay a premium for improved comfort (ca. €4,800), enhanced municipal energy advisory services (ca. €2,100), and higher CO2 savings (ca. €2,600). By contrast, they require substantial compensation for long payback times (ca. €7,500) and more disruptive retrofit works (ca. €1,100). These preferences are significantly moderated by individual behavioural biases: risk aversion and present bias are associated with lower willingness to pay for higher upfront costs, loss aversion is associated with stronger aversion to longer payback times, and status quo bias is associated with a stronger preference for municipal energy advisory services. Our findings underscore the importance of designing short-term, low-hassle retrofit offers that combine low-risk financial support with credible guarantees and low-disruption delivery models to accelerate the residential energy transition.

title: Research on the Impact of China's National Carbon Market on the Financial Performance of Listed Power Generation Firms
affiliations: Southern University of Science and Technology, Southern University of Science and Technology, Southern University of Science and Technology, Southern University of Science and Technology, Southern University of Science and Technology and Jiangsu Normal University

detail.title: Research on the Impact of China's National Carbon Market on the Financial Performance of Listed Power Generation Firms
detail.abstract: Emissions trading schemes (ETS) are an important market-based instrument for addressing climate change. However, evidence on the long-horizon, dynamic firm-level effects of China’s national emissions trading scheme (CN ETS) in the power sector remains limited. Leveraging the CN ETS launch as an exogenous shock, this study uses quarterly panel data on 79 listed power generation firms in China from 2016Q4 to 2025Q1 and applies a difference-in-differences framework to identify the policy impact of the CN ETS. We find pronounced temporal heterogeneity in the CN ETS effect on coal-fired power firms’ return on assets (ROA): ROA decreases by 0.734 % in the short run but turns positive in the long run, increasing by 0.254 %. Mechanism tests suggest that rising operating costs and declining market competitiveness are the primary short-run constraints, whereas an innovation compensation effect emerges over time and supports performance recovery in the long run. Heterogeneity analyses further show that the long-run performance recovery of coal-fired firms is more pronounced relative to hydropower firms than relative to non-hydro clean-energy generators, indicating that coal-fired firms’ cost and competitiveness disadvantages relative to the latter are more persistent. In thermal-power-dominant electricity markets, coal-fired firms exhibit no significant R&D response and experience more persistent competitiveness suppression; performance recovery relies more on cost-side easing and operational adjustments. In non-thermal-power-dominant regions, recovery depends more on R&D-induced green innovation, which in turn helps restore competitiveness. This paper provides evidence on the long-horizon dynamic effects of the CN ETS and informs ETS design and power-sector decarbonization policy.

reference: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1494
title: How do Immigrants Affect Local Public Finances? Evidence from Italian Municipalities
affiliations: Roma Tre University, Georgetown University - Department of Economics, University of Rome Tor Vergata - Faculty of Economics and Bank of Italy

detail.title: How do Immigrants Affect Local Public Finances? Evidence from Italian Municipalities

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bank of Italy Temi di Discussione (Working Paper) No. 1494
publicationDetails.journalName: Bank of Italy Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We estimate the causal impact of immigration to Italy on local public finances, at the municipality level (Comuni), between 2008 and 2015. We find that, with the arrival of immigrants, total (current plus capital) revenues go up, while total expenditures do not change, giving rise to an increase in the surplus of the municipality (all outcome variables in the paper are defined in per capita terms). We show that, in Italy, immigrants contribute to the broadening of the property tax base. They cause an increase in property tax revenues from “secondary residences”, which are often rented out and are subject to property taxation unlike owner-occupied units. On the expenditure side, immigrant inflows lead to greater current spending in total and on garbage collection, local police, cultural programs, and public transportation. Instead, capital expenditure decreases when immigrants arrive.

title: Marginal curtailment under network constraints: evidence from the 2030 GB power system
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Cambridge

detail.title: Marginal curtailment under network constraints: evidence from the 2030 GB power system
detail.abstract: High Variable Renewable Electricity (VRE) penetration inevitably leads to curtailment (shedding), typically measured by average curtailment. Marginal curtailment (mc, the fraction of potential output curtailed by the last MW) can be many times higher, raising the long-run marginal cost of investment, proportional to 1/(1-mc). A unit commitment and economic dispatch model of Britain, divided into seven zones by transmission constraints in 2030, demonstrates that these constraints considerably increase mc compared to no congestion, despite the considerable planned expansion of transmission, interconnectors, and storage that mitigates curtailment. The current auction design favours levelised costs, ignoring curtailment, but long-run marginal costs may be 90% higher, suggesting the need for careful locational planning and VRE support design.

reference: Duke Law School Public Law & Legal Theory Series Forthcoming
title: Pigou-Dalton and Separability: Is Equity-Regarding Moral Betterness Separable Across Persons?
affiliations: Duke University School of Law and University of Tokyo

detail.title: Pigou-Dalton and Separability: Is Equity-Regarding Moral Betterness Separable Across Persons?

publicationDetails.detailsText: Duke Law School Public Law & Legal Theory Series Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Duke Law School Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The Separability axiom (shorthand for person-separability) arises frequently in the literature on social choice and formal ethics. It is a fixed-population axiom (an axiom that constrains the ranking of a pair of worlds in which the very same individuals exist), which says: If some individuals are equally well off in the two worlds, the moral ranking of the two is independent of those individuals’ well-being levels. Variable-Population Separability is a logically stronger version of Separability that applies to any pair of worlds. It says: if some individuals are equally well off in the two worlds, the moral ranking of the two is independent of those individuals’ well-being levels and their existence.
The question of Separability has often been tied up with utilitarianism. A utilitarian world-ranking satisfies Separability; thus, an argument for utilitarianism is, automatically, an argument for Separability.

This paper engages Separability from a different angle. It starts from the Pigou-Dalton axiom: the standard axiom expressing a concern for the equitable distribution of well-being. The Pigou-Dalton axiom states: a pure, gap-diminishing transfer of well-being from someone better off, to someone worse off, leaving everyone else unaffected, is a moral improvement. Utilitarianism violates Pigou-Dalton.

Notably, Pigou-Dalton itself is neutral on the issue of Separability. Some prominent Pigou-Dalton-respecting world-rankings satisfy Separability (in particular, prioritarianism, leximin, and Pigou-Dalton-respecting sufficientarianism), while others do not (in particular, generalized Gini-world/rank-weighted world-rankings). The paper reviews and critically evaluates the main arguments for and against Separability, given the non-utilitarian concern for equity embodied in the Pigou-Dalton axiom. This is an important topic for social choice theorists and ethicists who endorse that axiom—and a topic that has not, to date, been systematically addressed. The paper reaches a tentative conclusion in favor of Separability, but defending that conclusion is not its main ambition. Rather, it chiefly aims to foster robust debate about whether Separability aligns with non-utilitarian, Pigou-Dalton-respecting, moral value.

title: Market Distortions in the Transport Sector of Bulgaria Influenced by the Activity of State-Owned Enterprises
affiliations: University of National and World Economy (UNWE) - Department of Economics and Economic Research Institute, Bulgarian Academy of Sciences

detail.title: Market Distortions in the Transport Sector of Bulgaria Influenced by the Activity of State-Owned Enterprises
detail.abstract: Some segments of the transport sector in Bulgaria are strongly dominated by state-owned enterprises (railway, maritime and inland waterway transport). This fact leads to distortions in the free competition conditions and then questions arise as to how justified the state intervention in these segments is. The publication studied the efficiency of the state-owned enterprises in the context of public priorities, which are pursued through these enterprises’ functioning. For the purposes of the present study, the institutional method is used, which is also combined with statistical analysis, focused on key indicators for efficiency measurement. As a result of the research, the level of enterprises’ innovation is evaluated, together with the level of efficient financial sources absorption by the National recovery and resilient plan, euro funds, operational programs and state budget transfers. The results of the research show that it is necessary to be rethought the concept for domination of the state-owned enterprises in the studied segments of the transport sector in Bulgaria. They must be open to competition, including foreign private companies. The innovation potential of these enterprises is low, which corresponds to the low financial sources’ absorption by the European funds as main beneficiaries of them.

title: The Dollar Value of Better Ad Content: Tracing the Relationships Between Ad Creatives, Ad Skipping, and Ad Elasticities
affiliations: University of Toronto, Southern Methodist University (SMU) - Marketing Department,  and Northeastern University - D'Amore-McKim School of Business

detail.title: The Dollar Value of Better Ad Content: Tracing the Relationships Between Ad Creatives, Ad Skipping, and Ad Elasticities
detail.abstract: What is the relationship between ad skipping behavior, ad creative attributes, and ad purchase elasticities? Using linked data on store revenues, television advertising, ad skipping behavior, and hand-coded ad creative attributes for 60 brands across 4 years, we estimate 1) the effect of ad skipping rates on ad elasticity, 2) the effects of different ad creative attributes on ad elasticity, controlling for ad skipping rates, and 3) the effects of different ad creative attributes on ad skipping rates. To overcome confounding, we use an instrumental-variables strategy to identify ad skipping rate effects and recover large estimated effects of skipping rates on elasticities: we find significantly positive ad elasticities for ads with average (or lower) ad skipping rates, but near-zero elasticities for ads with ad skipping rates one standard deviation above the mean. We then show that call-to-action and sensory features both have significant direct effects on ad elasticities, but only sensory features produce secondary purchase effects channeled through impacts on ad skipping rates. We use these estimates to quantify the total dollar-value impact of lower ad skipping rates and different creative attributes in ads, and demonstrate that high skipping rates may explain ad ineffectiveness for up to 32% of brands.

title: Impact of AI Search Summaries on Website Traffic: Evidence from Google AI Overviews and Wikipedia
affiliations: and University of Washington

detail.title: Impact of AI Search Summaries on Website Traffic: Evidence from Google AI Overviews and Wikipedia
detail.abstract: Search engines increasingly display LLM-generated answers shown above organic links, shifting search from link lists to answer-first summaries. Publishers contend these summaries substitute for source pages and cannibalize traffic, while platforms argue they are complementary by directing users through included links. We estimate the causal impact of Google's AI Overview (AIO) on Wikipedia traffic by leveraging the feature's staggered geographic rollout and Wikipedia's multilingual structure. Using a difference-in-differences design, we compare English Wikipedia articles exposed to AIO to the same underlying articles in language editions (Hindi, Indonesian, Japanese, and Portuguese) that were not exposed to AIO during the observation period. Across 161,382 matched article-language pairs, AIO exposure reduces daily traffic to English articles by approximately 15%. Effects are heterogeneous: relative declines are largest for Culture articles and substantially smaller for STEM, consistent with stronger substitution when short synthesized answers satisfy informational intent. These findings provide early causal evidence that generative-answer features in search engines can materially reallocate attention away from informational publishers, with implications for content monetization, search platform design, and policy.

title: Maryam Mirzakhani: A Luminous Mind in the Landscape of Mathematics
affiliations: Artificial Intelligence in Finance Institute

detail.title: Maryam Mirzakhani: A Luminous Mind in the Landscape of Mathematics
detail.abstract:
This book provides a comprehensive examination of the life, career, and enduring mathematical legacy of Maryam Mirzakhani (1977–2017). It traces her development from her formative years in Tehran—including her historic performance at the International Mathematical Olympiad—to her transformative doctoral studies at Harvard and her subsequent professorships at Princeton and Stanford.

The work explores Mirzakhani’s revolutionary contributions to Riemann surfaces and moduli spaces, detailing her recursive techniques for computing Weil-Petersson volumes, her breakthrough results on counting simple closed geodesics, and her geometric proof of Witten’s conjecture. Additionally, it examines the "Magic Wand Theorem"—the result of a decade-long collaboration that classified orbit closures for the $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ action on the moduli space of holomorphic differentials. Beyond her technical achievements, the book reflects on Mirzakhani’s unique methodology, characterized by visual intuition and persistence, and assesses her ongoing impact as the first woman to be awarded the Fields Medal.

reference: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper No. 1
title: Cheapflation Cycles
affiliations: Harvard University

detail.title: Cheapflation Cycles

publicationDetails.detailsText: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper No. 1
publicationDetails.journalName: Kilts Center at Chicago Booth Marketing Data Center Paper Series

detail.abstract: We document a new source of fluctuations in inflation inequality. When the cost of upstream inputs rises, varieties within a product category tend to have similar absolute price increases. However, the same absolute price increase constitutes a larger percentage change for low-price products, resulting in excess inflation at the low end ("cheapflation"). Since low-income households tend to buy lower-priced varieties, the inflation rates they face are disproportionately sensitive to upstream costs. Using data on food-at-home purchases, we show that this mechanism generates cycles in inflation inequality and excessive volatility in inflation for low-income households relative to high-income households. This channel parsimoniously accounts for observed fluctuations in inflation inequality over time, including surges in cheapflation and inflation inequality during both the Great Recession and the 2021-2023 post-pandemic inflation. Official statistics mask these within-category differences in inflation and thus understate the differences in inflation experienced by low-and high-income households by 70-90 percent. We provide evidence that this mechanism applies to a range of consumption categories beyond food at home. The same mechanism also leads to systematic differences in inflation across cities and import price inflation across countries in response to nationwide and global cost shocks.

title: AI in the Lab: AlphaFold2’s Impacts on Human-Produced Knowledge

detail.title: AI in the Lab: AlphaFold2’s Impacts on Human-Produced Knowledge

declarations.funderStatement: This work is partially funded by the Schmidt Sciences AI at Work program.

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates how Artificial Intelligence (AI) shapes scientific knowledge production by human researchers, taking Google’s AlphaFold2 (AF2) as a case. AF2 predicts protein structures with near-experimental accuracy at a fraction of the cost. Exploiting variation in AF2’s prediction confidence in a difference-in-differences design, I find that experimental output for well-predicted proteins falls by about 35%. This decline is more pronounced for proteins that are costly to experiment on or have limited downstream demand. The reallocation of effort is also heterogeneous across experimental methods, concentrated in widely accessible X-ray crystallography while leaving the capital-intensive cryo–electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) method largely unaffected. Meanwhile, AF2 has little effect on the quality of execution but appears to alter incentives: the academic reward for working on experimentally unattempted but well-predicted structures largely disappears, as reflected in a sharp drop in the probability of publication in top-tier journals. Overall, AF2 shifts experimental effort toward not-well-predicted areas where human comparative advantage persists.

title: AI Skills Improve Job Prospects: Causal Evidence from a Hiring Experiment
affiliations: University of Oxford - Oxford Internet Institute, University of Copenhagen - Copenhagen Center for Social Data Science and Oxford internet Institute

detail.title: AI Skills Improve Job Prospects: Causal Evidence from a Hiring Experiment

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics reference: Oxford Internet Institute (OII) DREC - 2006498
declarations.funderStatement: Microsoft AI Economy Institute

detail.abstract: The growing adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies has heightened interest in the labour market value of AI-related skills, yet causal evidence on their role in hiring decisions remains scarce. This study examines whether AI skills serve as a positive hiring signal and whether they can offset conventional disadvantages such as older age or lower formal education. We conduct an experimental survey with 1,700 recruiters from the United Kingdom and the United States. Using a paired conjoint design, recruiters evaluated hypothetical candidates represented by synthetically designed résumés. Across three occupations-graphic designer, office assistant, and software engineer-, AI skills significantly increase interview invitation probabilities by approximately 8 to 15 percentage points. AI skills also partially or fully offset disadvantages related to age and lower education, with effects strongest for office assistants, where formal AI certification plays an additional compensatory role. Effects are weaker for graphic designers, consistent with more skeptical recruiter attitudes toward AI in creative work. Finally, recruiters' own background and AI usage significantly moderate these effects. Overall, the findings demonstrate that AI skills function as a powerful hiring signal and can mitigate traditional labour market disadvantages, with implications for workers' skill acquisition strategies and firms' recruitment practices.

title: Information Provision and Market Thickness in Auctions: Evidence from the Online Ad Industry
affiliations: Duke University

detail.title: Information Provision and Market Thickness in Auctions: Evidence from the Online Ad Industry
detail.abstract: This paper studies how information provision shapes surplus and competition in market design by analyzing a tradeoff between matching and market thickness within the context of online advertising. Granular information allows advertisers to better identify high-value users, raising bids through better match, but enables them to enter fewer auctions, reducing competition. Using a dataset of 1.4 billion auctions, I estimate a model of advertiser entry and bidding with endogenous market thickness. Counterfactual simulations show that eliminating consumer-level information reduces ad spending by 65%, driven by an 89% decline from lower match, partially offset by a 24% increase from stronger competition.

title: How Should Content Creators Narrate Their Content? The Impact of Emotionality Flips on Audience Engagement
affiliations: , McGill University and ESSEC Business School

detail.title: How Should Content Creators Narrate Their Content? The Impact of Emotionality Flips on Audience Engagement
detail.abstract: The creator economy marks a pivotal shift in influencer marketing. Content creators create long content to engage their audience on social media platforms and generate revenue through engagement. We hypothesize that audience engagement with content is a function of emotionality flips: the number of times emotionality flips direction (from a positive to a negative slope, and vice versa) across one content unit (e.g., a sentence). Five studiesincluding 33,598 podcast episodes, 3,381 TED Talks, two lab experiments, and one synthetic validation-support this hypothesis. Furthermore, arousal is the underlying mechanism; that is, emotionality flips raise the audience's arousal, which in turn boosts audience engagement. Lastly, emotionality flips' positive effect is stronger for (1) content that is easier (vs. harder) to process, and (2) audiences with high (vs. low) need-for-affect. This research advances understanding of emotionality dynamics in the creator economy and offers insights for creators, platforms, and consumers.

title: Complementarity, Substitutability, and the Sustainability Halo: Evidence from a Synthetic-Agent Discrete Choice Experiment on Ecolabels, Brand Messaging, and Packaging
affiliations: Tennessee State University - College of Agriculture, Vanderbilt University - Medical Center and Tennessee State University

detail.title: Complementarity, Substitutability, and the Sustainability Halo: Evidence from a Synthetic-Agent Discrete Choice Experiment on Ecolabels, Brand Messaging, and Packaging

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Competing Interests: Author Abdelaziz Lawani, Author Anna Liisa Ihuhwa, and Author Armine Poghosyan declare none
declarations.ethicsApproval: This research uses Synthetic Agents, so no IRB approval is needed
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency, commercial or not-for-profit sectors

detail.abstract: Consumers are increasingly exposed to multiple sustainability signals, such as ecolabels, brand messaging, and packaging claims, that may reinforce or contradict each other. When ecolabels appear on environmentally inconsistent packaging, for instance, they can erode credibility and dilute consumer trust. This paper develops a theoretical and empirical framework to analyze how such informational cues interact in shaping consumer utility. Extending the economic concepts of complementarity and substitutability to the domain of sustainability signals, we examine whether multiple cues generate reinforcing (complementary) or redundant (substitutable) effects on perceived product value. Using a discrete choice experiment simulated with synthetic agents calibrated to U.S. consumer demographics and behavioral parameters, we test our theory by estimating multinomial and mixed logit models with cross-attribute interactions and randomized information treatments. Results reveal three key findings. First, willingness to pay for sustainability attributes is consistent with prior estimates in food labeling studies, $3.20 for pastureraised, $2.15 for organic, and $2.00 for sustainable packaging, and is highest when ecolabels appear on unsustainable packaging and diminishes when combined with other "green" cues, suggesting that contrast may amplify perceived value. Second, sustainability attributes display both complementarity and substitutability depending on domain overlap. Third, mid-task information boosts the valuation of environmental attributes while reducing reliance on brand heuristics. Methodologically, the paper demonstrates how synthetic agents can advance experimental economics by enabling scalable, reproducible modeling of preference structures.

title: AI and Skills-Based Hiring: Transforming Recruitment Practices

detail.title: AI and Skills-Based Hiring: Transforming Recruitment Practices
detail.abstract: This paper examines the shift from degree-based hiring to skills-based recruitment, driven by AI, workforce changes, and evolving business needs. Using a mixed-methods approach, the study analyzes quantitative data from industry reports and qualitative insights from HR executives at leading companies. It explores the drivers behind this transition, including the impact of AI on talent acquisition, the growing relevance of soft skills, and the role of digital platforms in providing alternative learning pathways. Despite its advantages, transitioning to skills-based recruitment presents challenges, including resistance from traditional businesses and ethical concerns related to AIdriven hiring processes. HR departments must invest in better assessment tools, while education providers should align curricula with industry demands. Additionally, the study highlights the challenges for universities, which must adapt to new demands by offering shorter, skill-focused learning models. As AI transforms hiring practices, businesses and education systems must collaborate to ensure a workforce equipped for future needs. Ultimately, this shift represents a long-term transformation rather than a passing trend. Embracing skill-based hiring can create a more inclusive, efficient, and competitive labor market, ensuring that organizations and employees remain agile in an era of rapid technological advancement. By embracing this evolution, organizations can better align talent with business needs, while professionals can leverage continuous learning to remain competitive in an AIdriven economy. The future of work is shifting-skills, not degrees, will be the new currency of success.

title: The Role of Time and Enjoyment in Consumers' Goal Progress Perceptions
affiliations: Cornell University, London School of Economics and Cornell University

detail.title: The Role of Time and Enjoyment in Consumers' Goal Progress Perceptions

publicationDetails.detailsText: JACR Volume 11, Number 3: Time in Consumption
Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Research Paper Forthcoming
publicationDetails.journalName: Cornell SC Johnson College of Business Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Consumers must invest time to make progress on a goal. Yet across nine studies (seven preregistered), including a supplemental study and post-test, consumers relied more on an activity's enjoyment than on perceived or actual time investment when judging goal progress. This effect arises because consumers hold two lay theories about progress: a time-progress lay theory and an enjoyment-progress one. Consumers rely more on the latter, in part because enjoyment is easier to evaluate and more attention-grabbing than time. For example, gym-goers believed they made more progress and burned more calories when exercise was more (vs. less) enjoyable, than when it felt longer (vs. shorter); similarly, increasing enjoyment of a skill-building task increased perceived skill development more than increasing task duration. These lay theories affect choice: consumers preferred a shorter, more enjoyable activity, unless the time-progress lay theory was activated and/or the diagnosticity of the enjoyment-progress lay theory was challenged.

title: From Adoption to Capability: Enterprise AI, Labor Structure, and Talent Constraints in the Philippines in a Global Context
affiliations: CirroLytix Research Services

detail.title: From Adoption to Capability: Enterprise AI, Labor Structure, and Talent Constraints in the Philippines in a Global Context
detail.abstract:
The Philippines has crossed a critical threshold in enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) adoption. Across industries and firm sizes, AI tools are now widely used, executive attention is sustained, and early productivity gains are evident. Yet global experience suggests that adoption alone does not translate into durable value. This paper argues that the Philippines now faces a more consequential challenge: scaling AI from widespread experimentation to institutionalized, enterprise-grade capability.

Drawing on two of the most comprehensive and recent studies on AI adoption in the Philippines—one enterprise-wide and one sector-specific to the IT-BPM industry—this paper synthesizes empirical evidence to assess the country’s structural readiness for AI at scale. Situating Philippine findings within global enterprise AI trends, the analysis shows that high experimentation combined with limited production deployment is not anomalous, but reflects a common “proof-of-concept trap” observed worldwide. However, the risks of stagnation are amplified in labor-producing economies.

The paper advances an original argument linking AI scaling constraints to the Philippines’ historical labor-export and labor-enabled services model. While this model has enabled rapid upskilling, adaptability, and early AI adoption, it has also produced thin layers of advanced technical, product, and governance capabilities—precisely the roles required to institutionalize AI systems. As global competition shifts from task execution toward system ownership and integration, these structural gaps become binding constraints.

The findings suggest that without deliberate investment in institutional depth—spanning talent development, data and integration infrastructure, and enabling governance—the Philippines risks remaining a consumer of AI tools rather than a builder of AI capability. The paper concludes by outlining strategic and policy implications for enterprises, the IT-BPM sector, and policymakers, emphasizing the need to move beyond adoption metrics toward sustained capability-building. The Philippine case offers broader lessons for labor-producing economies navigating the transition from labor arbitrage to AI-driven competitiveness.

reference: VOLUME 14 NO. 2 JULY-DECEMBER 2024 IPE Journal of Management
title: The Mediating Effect of Customer Satisfaction on the Relationship Between Brand Loyalty, Brand Awareness, and Customer Repurchase Intention with Reference to a D2C Brand
affiliations: Krea University

detail.title: The Mediating Effect of Customer Satisfaction on the Relationship Between Brand Loyalty, Brand Awareness, and Customer Repurchase Intention with Reference to a D2C Brand

publicationDetails.detailsText: VOLUME 14 NO. 2 JULY-DECEMBER 2024 IPE Journal of Management

detail.abstract: This study examines the mediating role of customer satisfaction in the relationship between brand loyalty, brand awareness, and repurchase intention within the Direct-to-Consumer (D2C) cookware industry, focusing on The Eco-friendly Cookware brand, using survey data from 156 customers analyzed through correlation and multiple linear regression (SPSS). The findings reveal strong positive relationships among all variables, with brand awareness (β = 0.530, *p* < 0.01) and customer satisfaction (β = 0.348, *p* < 0.01) as significant predictors of repurchase intention, demonstrating that customer satisfaction partially mediates the link between brand factors (awareness/loyalty) and repurchase behavior. Practical implications suggest D2C brands should enhance brand visibility and deliver exceptional customer experiences to foster loyalty, targeting environmentally conscious, financially stable, and educated consumers by highlighting eco-friendly benefits, improving brand visibility, and ensuring high satisfaction to strengthen market position and repurchase intention. This study contributes to the underexplored domain of D2C eco-friendly cookware by validating customer satisfaction as a mediator.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes a foundational principle for the governance of artificial intelligence systems used in decisions that affect rights, health, education, access, liberty, or the inclusion and exclusion of individuals: the Principle of Final Human Ratification. The principle establishes that no automated or algorithmic decision with significant human impact can be considered legally valid without the formal ratification of an identifiable human subject who explicitly assumes responsibility for the decision. It constitutes an ethical, legal, and institutional architecture designed to preserve moral imputability, the legal validity of decision-making acts, and the chain of responsibility in the age of algorithmic automation.

title: The Tragedy of Productivity: A Unified Framework for Diagnosing Coordination Failures in Labor Markets and AI Governance

detail.title: The Tragedy of Productivity: A Unified Framework for Diagnosing Coordination Failures in Labor Markets and AI Governance
detail.abstract:
We present a unified game-theoretic framework demonstrating that two seemingly distinct global failures (the structural decoupling of productivity gains from worker welfare and the acceleration of high-risk AI development) derive from an identical structural dilemma.

In 1930, John Maynard Keynes predicted that technological progress would reduce the working week to 15 hours by century's end. Despite productivity increasing eightfold since then, workers globally still work roughly double these hours. Separately, leading AI researchers warn of existential risks from artificial intelligence, yet development accelerates rather than slows. We demonstrate these failures share identical game-theoretic structure: coordination failures arising when individual rationality produces collective harm.

We synthesize from established game theory five necessary and sufficient conditions that characterize such coordination failures as structural tragedies: N-player structure with multiple independent actors, binary choices generating negative externalities, dominance property where defection yields higher payoffs, Pareto-inefficiency where cooperation dominates mutual defection, and enforcement difficulty from structural barriers. We extend this framework to quantify tragedy severity through condition intensities, introducing a Tragedy Index that reveals governance of transformative AI breakthroughs faces orders-of-magnitude greater coordination difficulty than historical cases including climate change, nuclear weapons, or bank runs. We validate this framework across canonical cases including commons tragedies, security dilemmas, bank runs, and space debris.

Applied to productivity competition, we prove firms face a coordination failure preventing productivity gains from translating fully to worker welfare. We show this formally for working hours; the same structural logic extends to wages, benefits, and job security. European evidence confirms that, even under maximally favorable institutional conditions, productivity welfare decoupling persists, manifesting differently across institutional contexts.

Applied to AI governance, we show development faces the same structure but with amplified intensity across eight dimensions compared to successful arms control cases, making coordination structurally more difficult than for nuclear weapons. The Russia-Ukraine drone war provides empirical validation: despite international dialogue on weapons governance, both sides escalated from dozens to thousands of drones monthly within two years, driven by competitive necessity that overwhelmed coordination aspirations.

The analysis is diagnostic rather than prescriptive: we synthesize from the literature structural barriers both to standard solutions and to the fundamental changes that would be required to resolve these tragedies, rather than proposing implementable solutions whose feasibility our framework questions.

title: Screening Precision, Loan Rates, and Credit Rationing in the Stiglitz--Weiss Regime

detail.title: Screening Precision, Loan Rates, and Credit Rationing in the Stiglitz--Weiss Regime
detail.abstract: Recent advances in underwriting methods, including credit scoring, alternative data, and automated verification, have increased the precision with which lenders infer borrower risk. This note studies how such improvements in informational precision affect equilibrium loan pricing and credit rationing in a Stiglitz-Weiss adverse-selection environment. Holding market structure fixed and allowing adverse selection to persist, we show that higher informational precision can increase the equilibrium profit-maximizing interest rate even though expected profits remain non-monotonic in the interest rate. The mechanism is local: improved precision weakens the marginal adverse-selection penalty from raising the interest rate, flattening the expected-profit schedule near its maximum and shifting the optimizer upward. We then show that, under a fixed lending capacity and a standard rationing-gap measure defined as excess demand at the equilibrium rate, improved precision can reduce measured rationing through equilibrium price adjustment. The note isolates this comparative static as a building block; a companion paper develops an approval-based rationing mechanism and applies the result to modern credit markets with underwriting technologies.

title: Sustainable AI: A Practitioner Framework for Energy-Efficient Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: Sustainable AI: A Practitioner Framework for Energy-Efficient Artificial Intelligence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable - this study did not involve human participants or experimental subjects
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this study

detail.abstract:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption is accelerating across industries, driving significant advances in productivity and innovation. However, the rapid scaling of AI systems has also introduced growing concerns around energy consumption, infrastructure strain, and environmental impact. This paper presents a practitioner-oriented framework for sustainable and energy-efficient AI, focusing on practical strategies that can be applied across the AI lifecycle—from model design and training to deployment and operations.

Drawing from real-world industry practices, the framework emphasizes energy-aware architecture choices, efficient model selection, cloud optimization, and governance mechanisms that align sustainability with performance and cost objectives. The paper further discusses why sustainable AI is increasingly relevant at a national scale, as AI workloads expand across critical sectors such as healthcare, finance, and public infrastructure. By framing energy efficiency as a first-class design consideration rather than an afterthought, this work aims to contribute to responsible AI adoption that supports long-term economic and environmental goals. The proposed approach is intended for practitioners, architects, and policymakers seeking scalable methods to reduce the energy footprint of AI systems without limiting innovation.

title: When Better Performance Feels the Same: Performance Underestimation in Human-AI Collaboration
affiliations: TUM School of Management,Technical University of Munich and

detail.title: When Better Performance Feels the Same: Performance Underestimation in Human-AI Collaboration
detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is improving employee performance and productivity across a wide range of tasks. However, little is known about how users subjectively evaluate their AI-augmented work. Drawing on the effort heuristic, which links perceived effort to perceived value, we hypothesize that individuals using AI may paradoxically underestimate their performance. Across three experimental studies (N = 932) involving management students (Studies 1 and 2) and full-time employees (Study 3), we find that although AI-assisted participants achieved significantly higher objective performance than unassisted participants, they systematically underestimated their performance, rating it lower than their objectively achieved outcomes. In contrast, unassisted participants exhibited no such underestimation. Importantly, this performance underestimation had downstream consequences: Participants receiving AI assistance (vs. no AI assistance) showed greater performance underestimation, which in turn predicted lower intentions to adopt the technology for work (Study 3). Together, these findings identify performance underestimation as a psychological barrier to AI adoption, suggesting that users fail to internalize objective performance gains and consequently undervalue their AI-assisted work.

title: Leveraging Peripheral Behavioral Signals to Predict Sparse Monetization Decisions: The Parallel Sequence Network
affiliations: Southern University of Science and Technology, University of Minnesota - Twin Cities - Carlson School of Management, Southern University of Science and Technology and Independent

detail.title: Leveraging Peripheral Behavioral Signals to Predict Sparse Monetization Decisions: The Parallel Sequence Network
detail.abstract: Data scarcity in labeled outcomes poses a fundamental challenge in predicting infrequent yet economically consequential human decisions, such as purchasing, subscribing, or gifting. Because these monetization outcomes are rare and costly to observe at the individual level, digital platforms often face severe shortages of reliable supervision signals. At the same time, platforms routinely collect abundant peripheral behavioral data that are unlabeled and only weakly correlated with monetization outcomes. Existing supervised prediction models that depend heavily on monetization labels tend to overfit to a small group of known spenders, struggle to generalize to users who have never monetized before, and suffer from delayed feedback and extremely imbalanced distributions. These limitations highlight a growing need for IS research on how to extract monetization-relevant signals from large-scale behavioral traces. To address this challenge, we propose a Parallel Sequence Network (PSN) that leverages abundant non-monetary engagement data to complement sparse monetization signals. Within the live-streaming context, PSN separately models short-term viewing behaviors to capture emerging interests and long-term gifting behaviors to preserve stable preference trajectories. A unified latent representation balances exploitation (repeated gifting to familiar channels) with exploration (interest in new channels) while mitigating the outsized influence of dominant high spenders. Furthermore, a two-phase transfer learning structure enables knowledge from viewing sequences to enhance monetization prediction for users with little or no monetization history. We evaluate the PSN framework using large-scale field data from a leading live-streaming platform in China. Results show that PSN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving key metrics (e.g., Hit Rate) by 3.6% to 191.7%. PSN demonstrates strong performance in early-stage spender identification and remains robust under severe class imbalance and temporal misalignment. We additionally demonstrate practical improvements in downstream tasks, including channel discovery and cold-start recommendations. This study contributes to IS research by establishing a scalable and generalizable approach for inferring value-creating intentions from weakly correlated peripheral behaviors, moving beyond outcome-only learning. Our findings also inform platform monetization strategies, offering data-driven guidance for resource allocation, traffic distribution, and sustainable growth in digital markets.

title: Enhancing Worker Productivity Without Automating Tasks: A Different Approach to AI and the Task-Based Model
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, University of Galway and Georgia Institute of Technology - Strategic Management Area

detail.title: Enhancing Worker Productivity Without Automating Tasks: A Different Approach to AI and the Task-Based Model

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The task-based approach has become the dominant framework for studying the labor-market effects of artificial intelligence (AI), typically emphasizing the replacement of human workers by machines. Motivated by growing empirical evidence that contemporary AI is more often used as a tool that augments workers, this paper develops two related task-based models in which AI enhances worker productivity without automating tasks. Abstracting from capital, we develop a pair of related task-based models that examine how technological progress in AI that provides new tools to augment workers affects aggregate productivity and wage inequality. Both models emphasize the role of human capital in intermediating the effects of AI-related technological shocks. In the first model, AI use requires specialized expertise, and technological progress expands the set of tasks for which such expertise is effective. We show that a larger supply of AI expertise amplifies the productivity gains from improvements in AI technology while attenuating its adverse effects on wage inequality. The second model focuses on non-AI skills, allowing AI tools to alter the set of tasks that workers can perform given their skills. In equilibrium, workers allocate across tasks in response to wages, generating an endogenous distribution of skills across the task space. A central result is that aggregate productivity and wage inequality depend on different global properties of this equilibrium distribution: productivity is particularly sensitive to thinly staffed tasks that create bottlenecks, while wage inequality is driven by the concentration of workers in a narrow set of tasks. As a result, improvements in AI tools can induce non-monotonic co-movement between productivity and inequality. By linking these mechanisms to multidimensional human capital---including AI expertise and higher-order non-AI skills---the paper highlights the role of education and training policies in shaping the economic consequences of AI-driven technological change.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

detail.abstract: Administrative data are used to establish patterns in contract terms, usage, and default rates of anonymized individual credit card accounts. The canonical heterogeneous-agent macro model is extended with a competitive credit card industry and ex-ante heterogeneity to explain these facts, including that the spread on card interest rates is several multiples of default rates. Some model implications of general interest are: (i) a 10 percent cap on credit card interest rates, as proposed in recent legislation, reduces credit limits for risky borrowers and is welfare reducing for them, and (ii) although most people are not liquidity constrained, the average model MPC is in the empirically relevant range because consistency with credit card facts implies people are impatient.

reference: FRB of Boston Working Paper No. 26-2
title: Merchant Steering of Consumer Payment Choice
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta and Federal Reserve Bank of Boston

detail.title: Merchant Steering of Consumer Payment Choice

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Boston Working Paper No. 26-2
publicationDetails.journalName: FRB-Boston: Research Department Working Papers (Topic)

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the degree to which merchants influence consumers’ choice of how they pay for transactions. Using data from the Survey and Diary of Consumer Payments Choice, we examine consumers’ adherence to their preferred payment method when making in-person transactions. We also investigate whether merchants are able to steer consumers away from their preferred payment method. We characterize preferences for paying with cash or cards according to consumers’ income, level of education, and employment status. We find that consumers make most payments with their preferred method. When consumers pay with a non-preferred method, it is due only in small part to merchants’ refusal to accept that payment method. If a merchant accepts card payments, consumers who prefer paying with cards are not likely to pay with cash for large-value transactions or for gas or groceries. Discounts on cash purchases do not affect the probability of consumers deviating from using cards and paying with cash. Finally, the paper identifies “inertia” effects, which lead consumers to use the same payment method for consecutive purchases.
